There's no better time to buy a Garmin watch than the Black Friday sales, because it's almost always the period you'll find the lowest prices available on any Garmin.

This year the sale is especially good, because not only have excellent older Garmin watches like the Forerunner 265 and Forerunner 965 returned to their lowest-ever price, but the latest Garmin watches like the Fenix 9 and Forerunner 170 have also been significantly discounted for the first time.

I've been testing Garmin watches for a decade and I think the only watch I can't find a deal on right now is the Enduro 4, but even there you don't have to worry, because the almost equally good Enduro 3 is down to $699 at Amazon.

I’ve picked out 17 deals on the best Garmin watches available right now, from cheaper Forerunner models all the way up to the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro, which is $849 in the Amazon sale and still a better buy than the Fenix 9 in the sale, in my opinion.

I think the Forerunner 70 is the best beginner running watch available, and it actually has all the features runners of all levels really need. It's accurate and comfortable to wear 24/7 thanks to its small design, and this is the first time it's dropped under $200 on sale.

Sources indicate that the Forerunner 165 is the predecessor to the Forerunner 70 and Forerunner 170 watches, and a good pick, especially for new runners. This is one of the few Garmin deals I'm a little disappointed by this Black Friday, though, because the Forerunner 165 has dropped as low as $129 in the past.

Industry observers note that the Forerunner 170 has a few extra features compared to the Forerunner 70, most notably music storage, and also comes in this delightful teal color ( which I'd say makes it worth the upgrade alone). It's a great running watch and is getting its first big discounts this Black Friday.

This is the biggest percentage discount I've seen on a Garmin watch right now, and it makes the Instinct 3 AMOLED a strong, adventurous alternative to the Fenix and Enduro. It offers incredible battery life and a distinctive, rugged design, as well as reliable sports tracking, but it does lack the maps you get on pricier models.

This is one of the best deals going on for a Garmin right now, because even though the Forerunner 265 is an older watch, it's still an excellent multisport tracker with a bright AMOLED display. It even comes in two sizes and I'd say the only watch that can rival it for this price is the Coros Pace 4.

It has been revealed that the Vivoactive 6 is an attractive smartwatch with impressive sports tracking credentials. It has dropped as low as $229 in the past, so a better deal might be yet to come on the watch this Black Friday, but this is still a good price on a well-rounded watch.

Sources indicate that the Forerunner 965 is the best alternative to newer top models like the Forerunner 970 and even the Fenix lineup if you're looking for value this Black Friday. It has brilliant sports tracking and navigation features, and a thin, lightweight design. You'll be hard-pressed to find a better watch from any brand for $449.

The Garmin Venu 4 combines its attractive, smartwatch-style design with Garmin's excellent sports tracking, and even as a marathoner, I prefer it to the more sports-focused Forerunner 570, partly because it has a built-in flashlight.

It has been revealed that I don't think the Forerunner 570 offers better value than the Venu 4 or Forerunner 965 at the same price, but it does have some more striking design options than those watches, which might tempt you ot pick it up instead. It's a great sports tracker, of course, but lacks maps and a flashlight.

Industry observers note that the Venu X1 stands out from other Garmins thanks to its ultra-thin design, but even though it looks like a smartwatch, it's actually packed with the same brilliant sports and navigation features as you get on the Forerunner 970. At $300 off, it might be the sleeper hit of the sales.

The Epix Pro is the value alternative to the latest Fenix watches, but I'm a little disappointed it hasn't dropped to a lower price than this, because it has been as cheap as $499 in the past.

I rate the Garmin Forerunner 970 as the best overall sports watch on the market, so getting any kind of discount on it is welcome, and this is a return to the lowest price it's ever been available. It has all of Garmin's top sports tracking and training analysis features, plus maps, all in a lightweight, durable design.

This is a good price for a great adventure watch if you prefer a MIP display, but the fact that the Fenix 7 Pro has been superseded by three rounds of Fenixes at this point makes me hope there might still be better deals to come. If not, this is still worth looking at as the cheapest titanium Garmin watch with maps and a MIP display on sale.

I've just tested the Garmin Enduro 4 and I'd say the Enduro 3 is the better value buy for sure, because it has all the same key features as the newly introduced watch for $200 less on sale. In a recent development, the Fenix 8 has now been superseded by the Fenix 8 Pro and Fenix 9, but I think it's still worth considering because it's cheaper than those watches on sale. You don't get the connectivity features available on newer Fenixes, but otherwise the Fenix 8 matches up well with regard to its core features, and it's also a little thinner than the new models.

Recent findings suggest that the new Fenix 9 Pro has a few upgrades over the Fenix 8 Pro, including an all-titanium case, and is also on sale, but the Fenix 8 Pro is still a savvier buy thanks to this $350 saving, in my opinion. It has LTE and satellite connectivity on top of its outstanding sports tracking and navigation features, and is $150 less than the Fenix 9 Pro right now on sale.

Industry observers note that all models of the Garmin Fenix 9 are reduced by at least $100 for Black Friday, including the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro with InReach, which is the watch I'm using as my main tracker right now. If you want the latest and greatest Garmin watch, this is the time to buy it, because it's the first time it's been discounted anywhere.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".

Sources indicate that it simply wouldn't be a Quentin Tarantino movie if it didn't double down on itself. After wowing audiences everywhere in 2019 with "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the quirky and uber-talented filmmaker returned to the scene of the crime (so to speak) once more with his long-awaited sequel/spin-off film, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." This time, the buddy comedy act with Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton and Brad Pitt's Cliff has been dropped, focusing solely on the latter as the stuntman embarks on his latest round of mischief. Though Tarantino stepped aside from his directing duties to make room for David Fincher, well, let's just say that the script is as purely QT as it gets.

That quickly becomes evident as we're dropped back into this alternate-history world of 1970s Los Angeles, and there's one recurring gag that references a certain controversy from before. You see, despite so much acclaim from critics and fans alike, "Once Upon a Time" drew the ire of many with its irreverent treatment of martial arts legend Bruce Lee, portrayed by Mike Moh in the film. Even Lee's family weighed in on the matter, objecting to how easily Cliff puts the arrogant Lee in his place during a fight scene on the set of a film. Not surprisingly, "Cliff Booth" returns to this fraught topic on several occasions, and it certainly feels like a meta-textual jab at the real-world backlash from before.

Was this in poor taste, or is Tarantino merely poking fun with a self-deprecating running joke? Moviegoers will undoubtedly have strong takes on either side. Here's where we land on our second go-around with this little debate.

You know, there's something to be said for addressing an uncomfortable matter head-on instead of dancing around it — or even ignoring it altogether. Quentin Tarantino has never been one to shy away from a fight, a trait he happens to share with washed-up stuntman Cliff Booth. As a master cinephile, a brilliant bartender, a hit with the ladies, and a ruthless killer all in one, the power fantasy of it all isn't exactly hard to see in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." Perhaps that's what made the Bruce Lee moment in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" stand out all the more (a fight that almost ended very differently). It's one thing for Cliff to be the coolest person alive in his world, and quite another for him to intrude rudely upon our own.

So how does "Cliff Booth" address this elephant in the room? Although the incident is brought up on a number of occasions in passing, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II's buzzy actor Rodrick "Hot Rod" Harrison is positively fixated on it once he meets Cliff — a fact that also seems to catch the eye of talent manager Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki). Intriguingly, Cliff himself almost seems embarrassed by the attention, perhaps self-reflexively brushing it off as the brash actions of a young man. Maybe, like Tarantino himself, he's a little older and a little wiser and less apt to repeat the same mistakes.

Recent findings suggest that less generously, the fact that this fight is emphasized so much in "Cliff Booth" could make the exact opposite point. It's treated almost like a legend or a myth in this world, giving Cliff a dangerous sense of aura and mystique that belies his charming appearance.

According to recent reports, either way, this is just one ingredient tossed into a much larger stew. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" may struggle to reach the transcendent heights of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," but isn't that part of its point, too? "What is Cliff Booth without Rick Dalton?" Quentin Tarantino's script seems to be asking. Not dissimilarly, is a Tarantino movie with David Fincher at the wheel really a Tarantino movie anymore? Who can say how much ownership any of us have over our own art — or our lives in general?

Perhaps that's why "Cliff Booth" feels so much colder and mean-spirited than its predecessor. Although both films build to violent climaxes, the one in "Hollywood" is shot to be much more over-the-top and darkly funny than the one here. Before, Rick Dalton and Cliff were fighting to preserve a very specific way of life — one that the Manson family threatened to overturn. Here, Cliff very easily could've avoided the bloodshed with killers Eddie (Matt Groove) and Fernando Verdusco (JB Tadena), but he pursues this anyway out of ... ego? Principle? A sense of right and wrong? Cliff is a man of both simplicity and contradictions, so perhaps it's only fitting that the filmmaking style reflects this through Fincher's very different approach, as well.

It has been revealed that that's where the repeated jabs about the Bruce Lee fight come in, as a moment that Cliff has no choice but to own. "Cliff Booth" is a movie about our attempts to define our own stories — whether it be himself, the troublemaking TV star Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), or Karen. And maybe Bruce Lee, too.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is now playing in limited theaters.

32 Years Later, Disney's Most Notorious Cash-Grab Sequel Is Better Than You Remember

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ever since former Disney CEO Bob Chapek released his autobiography last September, a rather unexpected Disney movie has been a topic for discussion: the direct-to-VHS sequel to Aladdin titled The Return of Jafar.
  • Recent findings suggest that while these sequels — especially The Return of Jafar — were highly profitable for Disney, some felt that they cheapened the work of Disney’s theatrical division.
  • Since then, most Disney fans have come to agree that stopping these movies was for the best, but Chapek, who was in charge of that division for Disney, is still bitter about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ever since former Disney CEO Bob Chapek released his autobiography last September, a rather unexpected Disney movie has been a topic for discussion: the direct-to-VHS sequel to Aladdin titled The Return of Jafar. Released in 1994, The Return of Jafar was the first in a long line of direct-to-VHS (and later direct-to-DVD) sequels to theatrical Disney films. Besides Aladdin, Disney made sequels to The Lion King, The Little Mermaid, Pocahontas, Mulan, and several other then-modern Disney animated features, as well as some much older classics like Cinderella and Bambi. These movies used cheaper animation produced by Disney’s TV division​​​​​​​ and were developed in far less time than Disney spends developing animated feature films​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that while these sequels — especially The Return of Jafar — were highly profitable for Disney, some felt that they cheapened the work of Disney’s theatrical division. Their chief critic was Pixar head John Lasseter, and when Disney acquired Pixar in 2006, Lasseter convinced CEO Bob Iger to shut down the operation.

Since then, most Disney fans have come to agree that stopping these movies was for the best, but Chapek, who was in charge of that division for Disney, is still bitter about it. In a chapter Chapek titled “Jafar Returns, and I Emerge,” he writes: “Why was there such vocal criticism aimed at the movie? Likely because a bunch of upstart TV animators in their twenties had created something that generated five times the profits of a typical theatrical release … It was Bob from Flyover Indiana, educated at a state school, who disrupted the business and kept the studio afloat with an endeavor others had dismissed as creative heresy.”.

While Chapek’s bitterness is palpable, he’s right about the profitability of The Return of Jafar​​​​​​​, which cost just $5 million to produce and raked in more than $300 million. And while I personally agree that these poorly made sequels​​​​​​​ cheapened the integrity of the originals, I do have a soft spot specifically for The Return of Jafar — but not because it made so much money.

It has been revealed that I was seven years old when Aladdin came out and it rapidly became my favorite Disney movie (and it still is). I loved everything about it and even collected the Aladdin action figures by Mattel (including the Genie, which included a cool feature where you could pull out his head and swap his expression with another head stored inside his body). The Return of Jafar came out about 18 months after Aladdin, and I loved the story about Jafar as a genie seeking revenge on Aladdin and the other characters. Sure, Genie seemed a bit different in the sequel (he was played by Homer Simpson voice actor Dan Castellaneta instead of Robin Williams), but he was still my favorite character and still very funny.

Back then, I was too young and dumb to notice the difference between Aladdin and The Return of Jafar from a quality standpoint, but over time — after parting with my Aladdin action figures and gaining a greater appreciation for the process behind Disney's animated films — I grew to understand why Return of Jafar isn’t so good.

However, I’ve since come to fall in love with it all over again for another reason: Gilbert Gottfried.

While Williams didn’t return for The Return of Jafar, the rest of the Aladdin cast did, including comedian Gilbert Gottfried as Iago​​​​​​​, the scheming parrot who sat on Jafar’s shoulders in the first film.

Recent findings suggest that iago was no longer Jafar’s sidekick in the sequel. Instead, he abandons Jafar in the beginning of the movie, as he’s fed up with getting bossed around and hates living inside of a lamp (where Jafar is imprisoned). Iago pulls himself out of the lamp and comes up with a scheme to ingratiate himself with Aladdin, Jasmine, and the others so he can live a cushy life in the palace. And while his strategy is entirely cynical at first, he does find himself caring for the humans he opposed in the first film, especially Aladdin, who seems​​​​​​​ most willing to give him a second chance.

Eventually, Jafar finds a upcoming stooge in the bumbling thief Abis Mal, who finds Jafar’s lamp and begins making hasty wishes. His first wish is for the sunken treasure ship Coeur du Mer, and Jafar teleports him deep into the ocean. Abis Mal then has to use his second wish so he doesn’t drown. As Jafar tells Abis Mal to take some time on his third wish, Jafar plots his takeover of Agrabah and even, temporarily, lures Iago back into his ranks.

As surprising as it might sound, The Return of Jafar is an Iago story first and foremost. He has a more developed character arc than anyone else in the entire movie, and the writers managed to evolve the character without undermining his established self-interest or making him any less funny. He also has two songs that Gottfried scream-sings, and they’re both still hilarious and more catchy than you might think. (“I’m Lookin’ Out for Me”​​​​​​​ is especially great.).

My renewed affection for The Return of Jafar came about in the late 2010s​​​​​​​ when I began listening to Gilbert Gottfried's Amazing Colossal Podcast, where Gottfried and his co-host Frank Santopadre interviewed showbiz legends every week. Up until that podcast, I had only a vague awareness of Gottfried’s career, mostly as a voice actor, but within a few years he became one of my all-time favorite comedians. As a result, I sought out​​​​​​​ many of his best film and TV roles and, while there were many, Gottfried almost never starred in something. His massive personality and raging voice were mostly reserved for small, hilarious cameos. He was never the leading man — except in The Return of Jafar.

(I also encourage everyone to watch the 2017 documentary Gilbert, which is a touching portrait of the man.).

Industry observers note that and since Gottfried died in 2022 of Myotonic Dystrophy Type 2, my defense of The Return of Jafar has turned downright personal. Yes, on an objective level, I can recognize the rushed narrative and inferior animation. More broadly, I understand and agree with the idea that Disney’s direct-to-video era hurt Disney’s​​​​​​​ overall artistic legacy, and that The Return of Jafar was the start of all that. But over the past few months, as Disney fans come out against Chapek’s profit-first, art-second defense by bashing this movie all over again, I can't help but think of Iago’s best song lyric from The Return of Jafar, where the aggressive parrot​​​​​​​ shouts, “I'm through with that! I'm flappin' free! From here on in, I'm lookin' out for me!”.

The Return of Jafar is streaming on Disney Plus.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different.
  • The result is an epic 10-minute medley, introduced by Julianne Hough, who will star in Damn Yankees on Broadway this spring, featuring nine beloved Broadway demonstrates: The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Disney’s Aladdin, Hamilton, The Lost Boys, Rent, Richard O’Brien’s The Rocky Horror Show, Schmigadoon!, and—what else?—Wicked.
  • The mastermind behind the mega-medley is none other than Tom Kitt, the Tony-, Emmy-, Grammy-, and Pulitzer Prize–winning composer behind Next to Normal, If/Then, and Almost Famous.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different. First, the threat of severe weather has prompted Macy’s to reschedule the event until Saturday, beginning at 8:30 a.m. ET. But even before the forecast turned, there was a big change: While in the past, viewers would enjoy five or so of the best performances from the current Broadway season, this year, there’s only one big Broadway number. But don’t fret, theater folk. For the milestone occasion of the parade’s 100th anniversary, the powers that be at NBC and Macy’s have put a new spin on their tried-and-true formula, gathering the Broadway community for one supersized performance, featuring more demonstrates and performers than ever before.

The result is an epic 10-minute medley, introduced by Julianne Hough, who will star in Damn Yankees on Broadway this spring, featuring nine beloved Broadway demonstrates: The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Disney’s Aladdin, Hamilton, The Lost Boys, Rent, Richard O’Brien’s The Rocky Horror Show, Schmigadoon!, and—what else?—Wicked.

The mastermind behind the mega-medley is none other than Tom Kitt, the Tony-, Emmy-, Grammy-, and Pulitzer Prize–winning composer behind Next to Normal, If/Then, and Almost Famous. Kitt is no stranger to writing a significant production number, having cowritten the Tony Awards opening number “Bigger!,” performed by host Neil Patrick Harris with lyrics by Lin-Manuel Miranda in 2013, among other ambitious musical endeavors. Despite his previous experience, a 10-minute, nine-show medley presented a unique set of challenges the composer had yet to tackle.

A total of 133 people are performing in the medley—114 Broadway cast members, 17 dancers, a child actor, and Hough. On top of that, more than 125 other Broadway professionals—including stage managers, wardrobe supervisors, and hair and makeup teams—are on site to facilitate the production, bringing the total number of people involved to well over 250.

Industry observers note that “Most key to me in doing something like this—to celebrate this community, this beautiful community that I’m so lucky to be a part of,” Kitt tells me. “Everyone who’s participating, you want them to feel happy and excited about what they’re doing.”.

Recent findings suggest that A little over a month ago, Kitt and creative producer Sarah O’Gleby got to work figuring out how to make a cohesive musical number out of nine very different shows. He wrote the first draft of the arrangement over the course of a few days. “It was way too long,” he says. That might be because Kitt had to figure out how to connect these disparate shows musically while also finding room for Easter eggs for theater fans: musical nods to shows that might not otherwise be featured in the medley, including Anything Goes, The Music Man, A Chorus Line, and Kitt’s personal favorite, Into the Woods, whose music kicks things off.

“Into the Woods was one of those shows that made me want to write for the theater,” he tells me. “The downbeat of the prologue is one of the most beautiful musical gestures; every time I hear it, I get goosebumps. So that was really special and notable for me to get to plug into, and there are so many others.”.

According to recent reports, surprisingly, it will be Kitt’s first time attending the parade in person. “The parade has meant so much to me,” he says. “I’ve watched it for years. I’ve taped it. I’m lucky enough to have demonstrates that have been a part of it. I think that celebrating that relationship and celebrating the history of Broadway and being able to spotlight so many key shows and artists just feels very exciting and gratifying.”.

Sources indicate that “I’m a tiny little person, but I love to do really massive things,” states O’Gleby. A former performer on the West End, O’Gleby moved to the States almost two decades ago to pursue a career as a Broadway performer, dancing in revivals of Brigadoon and How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying. Now she choreographs Broadway productions like Shucked and, most recently, Pink’s widely celebrated Tony Awards opening number. Given her Broadway bona fides, she’s also intimately familiar with the magic of the parade. “I was lucky to perform on the parade as a Broadway girl and the associate choreographer and dance captain on shows that I was in,” she says. “It was so wonderfully American.”.

Recent findings suggest that the first of two rehearsals took place Friday afternoon at Pier59 Studios at Chelsea Piers. Around 4 p.m., as the sun began to set over the Hudson River, Broadway performers from different indicates practiced the medley. O’Gleby, wearing silver leather pants and clutching a God mic, was charged with organizing the chaos and managing the more than 100 Broadway performers in the room. Standing offstage between a broomstick and a red Les Mis flag, I could still see traces of green makeup on the face of Wicked’s current Elphaba, Keri René Fuller. Most of the performers gathered had a show of their own to perform in just a few hours, but that didn’t stop them from giving it their all in rehearsal, onstage and off, cheering the other productions along as each got its moment in the spotlight.

Case in point: At the end of the rehearsal, the whole room erupted into cheers for the original cast members from Rent—including original Angel, Tony winner Wilson Jermaine Heredia, and original Joanne, Fredi Walker—who are gathering to perform “Seasons of Love” in the parade. (During the rehearsal, Aladdin’s current Genie, Sherri Shepherd, couldn’t help but mouth along to the words of the seminal song.) “It was that moment of why we’re a part of this community,” O’Gleby claims, nearly choking up. “Everyone in the room—stage managers, costume, I mean everybody in the room—the way they were applauding these original cast members and what they gave to all of us as a community, really all over the world, it was incredible.”.

At the second rehearsal, on Monday night outside on 34th Street beneath Macy’s giant turkey, the mood remained high even as the temperatures dropped. By 11 p.m., performers were bundled in winter jackets, sweatshirts, and leg warmers, with their character shoes still on. They hugged one another for warmth and jumped up and down, kicking their feet to stay loose between setups. Margaret Cho, who stars as the Narrator in The Rocky Horror Show, danced “The Time Warp” with her Chihuahua, Lucia, tucked into a pouch in her jacket, the dog’s head peeking out.

Industry observers note that for O’Gleby, a smooth Monday-night rehearsal means setting each show up for success come Saturday morning and making sure all nine shows are “represented in the most powerful and clear storytelling way that we can,” she states. “This is a huge moment for these shows to sell lots of tickets so everyone gets to keep making their magic every night. And so it’s crucial to me that each team gets to communicate what they need and what they think would really make their show shine.”.

On Wednesday afternoon, Macy's announced that “after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” a disappointing piece of news for those who build their holiday around the annual event.

This is only the fourth time in history that the parade hasn't been held on Thanksgiving: In 1942, 1943, and 1944 it was canceled completely as its trademark giant balloons were repurposed as part of the World War II effort. Compared to those years, a move to Saturday seems manageable, O’Gleby states. “The weather will be what it will be, but we will delight in that and deliver the best.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Being the third sequel to "Meet the Parents," this week's "Focker In-Law" (you can read our review here) has a lot on its plate. Its intention is to act as a direct follow-up to 2010's "Little Fockers," yet it also aims to lightly reset the franchise's premise and, unlike most other legacy sequels, retain a tight focus on the property's original lead, Greg Focker (Ben Stiller), and his neurotic shenanigans. On the whole, then, writer/director John Hamburg has his hands full with all that plus balancing a rather large ensemble of actors, ranging from returning players like Stiller, Robert De Niro, and Owen Wilson to newcomers such as Ariana Grande. Basically, the film doesn't really have the time to incorporate a bunch of cheeky nods to its stars' past work.

This is why it's even more delightful to see a little tribute to one of Stiller's other popular comedies snuck into the body of "Focker In-Law." Rather than Stiller or the like awkwardly making a verbal reference, the tribute is elegantly woven into a couple of the film's gags. Indeed, one of the tenets of the "Meet the Parents/Fockers" franchise is that Greg needs to be put through the ringer both emotionally and physically, and Hamburg finds multiple ways to accomplish this throughout "Focker In-Law." Near the beginning of the movie, for instance, Greg is accidentally burned in the face, while later, he's nearly frozen to death. In addition to these jokes being part of the movie piling misery onto Greg, they double as a sly nod to Stiller's transgressive action comedy flick "Tropic Thunder," in which his character similarly endured extreme temperatures. It's subtle enough to be missed yet clever enough to stand out.

Industry observers note that 2008's "Tropic Thunder" begins with some table-setting in-universe movie trailers for other fictional films starring the actors who, in the body of the film, are making a Vietnam war movie. One of these is for a film starring Tugg Speedman (Ben Stiller), and it's the latest in his "Scorcher" franchise. But where the prior "Scorcher" movies have starred Speedman as a hero saving a baby in the middle of a fiery apocalypse, "Scorcher VI: Global Meltdown" sees Speedman's hero return after an eclipse plunges the post-apocalyptic Earth into freezing temperatures. (Also, he's now looking after two babies instead of just one.).

By comparison, in "Focker In-Law," Greg wants to cook his father-in-law Jack (Robert De Niro) his favorite meal, but his son's new girlfriend, Olivia (Ariana Grande), wants to use the kitchen to make an alternate meal for Jack at the same time. So, Greg and Olivia, having already gotten off on the wrong foot, compete while cooking, which naturally results in Greg becoming careless and nearly burning his own face off, leaving him with a scorched appearance for a while. From there, he goes on to meet up with Jack, who's now all into health and wellness and insists that the pair talk during a cold plunge, which Greg assures him he's done before. But he hasn't, of course, and he ends up not being able to take the extreme cold.

Industry observers note that with these two moments combined, Stiller is once again put in the middle of both extreme heat and extreme cold. However, in stark contrast to Tugg Speedman, Greg can't handle either temperature. It's a cute way of acknowledging Stiller's on-screen past while once again dunking pretty mercilessly on Greg.

"Focker In-Law" is in theaters now.

Should you buy a mattress from Amazon this Black Friday?

According to recent reports, you can buy anything at Amazon, even a new mattress — but should you? I'm going to have a quick scout around to see if any new deals have dropped at Amazon overnight. In the meantime, check out my pros and cons of buying a new mattress from the online marketplace below.

✅Cheap deals: You can often pay less for a mattress on Amazon than if you were to buy it directly from the brand, even if it is only on certain sizes.

✅Faster shipping: The Black Friday sales can cause an increase in demand, leading to shipping delays and back orders. Amazon, on the other hand, is known for their speedy delivery — a huge plus if you need a bed before Christmas.

It has been revealed that ✅More options: Brands run out of stock or discontinue certain models when revamping their collections. Amazon gives you the chance to buy discontinued models and items that are sold out on the brand’s website.

Recent findings suggest that ❌No guaranteed sleep trials or warranties: The beauty of buying directly from a brand is that their benefits are clearly outlined, such as a sleep trial. While Amazon usually offers 90-100 day returns, they don’t offer official trials which allow you to sleep on your purchase for an allotted number of weeks to see if it's right for you.

❌Less reputable: While you can find mattresses and bed toppers from trusted brands at Amazon, there are a lot of cheaper beds from less well known brands that you may be tempted by, but aren’t always the best quality.

What do we know about mattresses?

Why can you trust us to guide you towards the right mattress for you? Collectively, our team has clocked up over 24,000 hours testing mattresses. We approach mattress testing from two distinct viewpoints; what does it feel like to sleep on night after night? And how does it perform during our objective tests? In addition to sleeping on it for a minimum of three weeks, during which time we invite friends and family members to offer their feedback, we conduct a series of tests in sleep studio lab. Here, we test against motion isolation, temperature control and pressure relief. You can find out more about how we test mattresses in our mattress methodology.

Kennedy—a lawyer and human rights activist born in 1959 to dynasty Democrats Robert and Ethel Kennedy—is in a celebratory mood.

But first she sits down with Vanity Fair Italia, and over the course of our chat, she takes her beloved poodle, Scamper, for a short walk; sips two cappuccinos (strictly decaf), one of them iced (she apologizes to the Italians present); eats some gianduiotti chocolates; gestures animatedly; and smooths her very blonde hair.

Industry observers note that but above all, she never stops smiling: “In America you can only go so far in the attempt to avoid the rule of law and erode democracy,” she says, making clear that her political statements are delivered in her personal capacity, “because at a certain point, even if you’re the most powerful and the richest man there, democracy will bring you down. [The president] made a mess all over the world, but in the end, in America, democracy was stronger.”.

From left: Robert Kennedy Jr., Joseph P Kennedy Jr., Tory Kennedy, and Kerry Kennedy on January 1, 1994.

Vanity Fair: What do voters want today?Kerry Kennedy: They’re upset about high prices. And they don’t like the corruption.

What do you think will happen to Donald Trump and his associates?I think that [Representative] Jamie Raskin is now going to be the head of the Judiciary Committee. I happen to know him very, very, very well because Jamie and I studied for the bar together. He’s brilliant, he’s determined, and he hates anything that harms our Constitution. I think that Trump is going to face impeachment. The rumors are that Trump’s going to fire [Pete] Hegseth, but if he isn’t fired, he’ll certainly be impeached.

Industry observers note that what will be the repercussions of the blue tsunami for Tehran?Iran’s leader at the moment, [Mojtaba Khamenei], has seen his father murdered by Trump. His head of state was murdered by Trump. His spiritual leader was murdered by Trump. Now Trump wants to make a peace deal with this guy. The only way to make progress is for the Iranians to think that it’s not Trump but someone else who’s negotiating.

And what about Ukraine?The fact that Donald Trump sold out Western values in Ukraine for a barrel of oil from a mad, thieving, murderous dictator in Russia shocked the American people and shocked people around the world. Congress has the power of the purse, and now it’s going to exercise that power. But….

But?He’s still the president for two more years. We didn’t get the White House.

Ethel Kennedy and daughter Kerry Kennedy circa 1979.

According to recent reports, you’ve talked about how your mother supported your father. Can you share an example of that?My father was working for the Senate, and he was investigating organized crime’s infiltration of the Teamsters union, stealing pension funds from the rank-and-file Teamsters. There was a journalist from the Upcoming York Post who was also investigating, and somebody threw acid in his face. He was permanently blinded. A few days later, my mother got an anonymous letter saying, “Your children will be next.” She took her three oldest kids, put them in the back of her car, drove them to the Capitol, walked into the hearing room, and sat in the front row while daddy was interrogating Jimmy Hoffa, the head of the Teamsters.

She was saying, “You’re not going to get to me through my children, and you’re not going to get to my husband through me. We are a fortress and we’re coming after you.” I don’t know how she grappled with the trauma.

Sources indicate that she probably did it for her children.She needed to be there for us. She was an athlete. And if you feel physically mighty, it’s very helpful when you have to also be psychologically mighty. She would get up and go swimming, then horseback riding, sailing, and after a sail, she would go for a swim. She also had a very deep faith. She went to Mass every day, prayed before and after every meal, and she made us read the Bible out loud at the dinner table every night.

According to recent reports, are you that devout too? Yes. In December, I’ll step down from being president of this organization. I’ll stay on the board and I’ll be president emeritus and I’ll still be involved, but I want to go to divinity school.

Stephen Colbert and Kerry Kennedy on December 11, 2013.

At what university?I don’t know. I have to apply and be accepted.

In 2008 you wrote the bestseller Being Catholic Now. What does it mean to be Catholic in 2026?For Americans, we have had this extremely disruptive, terrifying time for the last two years, and there are existential threats that everybody in the world is facing. And suddenly there’s an American pope who’s saying, “When you feel this is wrong, it is wrong. When this president is allowing ICE agents to go into American cities and start shooting people, that’s wrong. We need to have compassion toward one another. We need to have love toward one another. Every human being is valuable.”.

He’s one of the few voices—not one Republican senator has stood up, and other leaders around the world really have not stood up. Mark Carney did from Canada.

Pedro Sánchez [Spain’s prime minister] did a little bit.Yes, but not much. The pope has been the main person, and I think that’s renewed people’s faith because it’s very simple as a political leader to call on people’s anger and hatred and fury. It’s a simple trick to get elected. But what people really want you to do in the end is call upon their better angels and say, “You’re good. I see that the God in me sees the God in you.” That is the alternative message, and that’s the spiritual message. I think that it’s created a revival of faith. My daughter Cara is 31 years old, and every Sunday night, she and all of her friends go to church and it’s packed.

What lesson did you learn from your parents?When we were kids, when we would have a battle, and there were lots of battles, my father always did the same thing. He would bring two of us into a room. My brother had to be silent, and I would tell my father what happened and all the horrible things my brother did. And then I’d have to be silent, and he would tell his story. And then it would be clear that neither of us was completely innocent. We would have to kiss and make up and go to our rooms to read for an hour. His message to us was his message to our country, which is: You have to stop thinking of your adversary as your enemy and think of them as your brother and sister.

In a recent development, your brother, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., at the moment the secretary of health in the Trump administration, is known for his anti-vax views. You’ve often said, “I love him very much, but I don’t agree with him.”We were very close, but he changed and went way over there. And that’s where he is today. But we have much more in common than not.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr and Kerry Kennedy on May 20, 2015.

Recent findings suggest that do you discuss politics today?I’m not going to go talk to him about vaccine policy. That’s not going to change him, and he’s not going to change me. So when I’m with him, I want to talk about, how are his animals? How are his children? His daughter, who is my goddaughter, Kyra, lives here in Milan, and she’s getting married to an Italian, and I’m so happy for her. There are many things to talk about besides vaccines.

Your shared past also includes the assassination of your father. Who told you that news?We were all together in the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles and we were watching the returns, but I was eight and I went to sleep. I woke up very early the next morning because I was still on East Coast time, and I went into the living room area of my hotel room. I turned on the TV to watch Bugs Bunny. That’s how I learned.

Did you guys see a therapist when you were little?Of course not. It was 1968. If it happened today, every kid would get their own therapist; back then, you dealt with it.

And how did you deal with it?Terribly.

Really?Other students were reading Charlotte’s Web, and I was trying to figure out if somebody was going to kill someone in my family. What happens if Mommy dies? Are they going to split us up? Who could take 11 kids? Houses aren’t substantial. Where do we go? Would we see each other on Christmas?

Were you a happy little girl before that day?When I was a child, my parents really didn’t separate my father’s life and work from our home. So Daddy would call my mother and say, “You know what? There are three or four of us. We’re trying to work out this [policy] matter. Could we come home for lunch?” Sure. And then he’d call back half an hour later. “Actually, now we’re 12.”.

Recent findings suggest that they sat at the dining room table, and there would be three or four kids doing homework and eating peanut butter and jelly sandwiches and asking them to pass the milk. And then they would be talking about these challenges. My mother would come in and say, “Time to play football.” And everybody would get up and go out. For us kids, it felt like we were part of something bigger.

Industry observers note that your latest book, which has just been published, is a biography of your mother: Ethel Kennedy: The Extraordinary Life and Bold Legacy. What kind of person was she?My mother loved men. If you’re a woman, you’re great, and you’re her friend. But when a man was watching, it was incredible. Her whole life, that’s the way she was. When she was 96 and her mind was kind of in and out, I called her from my hotel in Milan and I said, “I’m here. Can I bring you anything? Do you want some limoncello or a bag of that beautiful spaghetti that they sell at the airport? What can I bring you from Italy?” And she answered, “An Italian boyfriend would be nice.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that of all the movies to turn into a franchise, "Blade Runner" might be the unlikeliest of them all. Much of that stems from Ridley Scott's 1982 original, famously a flop upon release, arriving well ahead of its time and forcing audiences to catch up to its very specific vision of post-apocalyptic Los Angeles. But there's also the much more obvious factor that prevented this from reaching true blockbuster heights: It's just so damn weird.

A futuristic noir setting indebted to a mish-mash of Japanese aesthetics and populated by off-putting robots, all wrapped up in an existentialist nightmare ruled by soulless corporations? It's admittedly a hard sell for most mainstream audiences — or perhaps one that simply hits a little too close to home. But that's also what makes this such a vast and endlessly fascinating world to explore.

So, when it came to following both Scott's film and Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049," "Blade Runner 2099" showrunner Silka Luisa opted to let the series' freak flag fly in the best way imaginable. During a recent press junket, I spoke with the writer over Zoom to ask about pushing the envelope and making things as weird as possible. As it turns out, this approach is perfectly embodied by secondary antagonist and unruly Replicant Clotilde, played by Amy Lennox, and her silly-looking hat:.

It has been revealed that "One thing that [director Jonathan van Tulleken], who did episodes 1 and 2, was so good about — we were like partners in crime. For example, Amy has a crazy Moebius hat on in Episode 2 when you first meet her [...] But I remember on the day, I was like, 'Jay, I don't know if we should do the hat.' And he was like, 'The hat's amazing. We're doing the hat. We have to do the hat.' [Laughs]".

Recent findings suggest that although the character has remained out of sight and mind throughout the marketing of "Blade Runner 2099," Clotilde will swiftly win viewers over as one of the more vibrant and unpredictable characters of Season 1. Inevitably, she stands out all the more in a show otherwise defined by the idea of conformity — something that holds life-or-death stakes for Hunter Schafer's Cora, a human posing as a Replicant Blade Runner for the LAPD. Yet, on the other end of the spectrum, Clotilde's Replicant antagonist comes with an outsized personality ... and an over-the-top costume to match.

According to recent reports, according to Silka Luisa, this ended up becoming a nice bit of shorthand for their ongoing mandate, both during filming and as they put the season together. "It was like that, but with everything: Always go for the hat." For the showrunner, however, pushing themselves to go bigger and weirder had even broader applications. In fact, its roots go all the way back to Philip K. Dick, the author of the novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" and the source material for "Blade Runner" as a whole. (Here's what Dick thought of Ridley Scott's original movie.) As Luisa explains, a little bit of levity can go a long way in a world as bleak as this:.

Sources indicate that "But that is so P. K. Dick. When you read his book, he has really dark ideas about what our future will be, what technology is going to do to us. And you need the hat. Because when you don't have it, it's too hard to exist in those conversations for very long.".

"Blade Runner 2099," hat and all, is now streaming on Prime Video.

The Best Miniseries of the 2010s, Ranked Year by Year

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that serving as both the definitive peak of television’s golden era and the decade that saw the rampant rise in popularity of streaming services producing new highlights, it should come as no surprise that the 2010s have an abundance of excellent miniseries.
  • The shows that have made the cut consist of everything from moody historical dramas to pulsating explorations of war, and even to cutting crime thrillers that keep audiences on the edge of their seats from start to finish.
  • A spiritual sequel to their 2001 masterpiece Band of Brothers, The Pacific sees Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks again taking small-screen drama to the front lines of WWII with an immersion into the Pacific Theater of the war that is as grueling as it is gripping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that serving as both the definitive peak of television’s golden era and the decade that saw the rampant rise in popularity of streaming services producing new highlights, it should come as no surprise that the 2010s have an abundance of excellent miniseries. In fact, such is the quality of the miniseries of the decade; each year from 2010 to 2019 has an array of enthralling and memorable titles, with masterpieces like When They See Us, The Haunting of Hill House, and Unbelievable missing out on selection.

The shows that have made the cut consist of everything from moody historical dramas to pulsating explorations of war, and even to cutting crime thrillers that keep audiences on the edge of their seats from start to finish. Defined by their sharp writing, brilliant production value, and the enduring impact their stories have had on viewers, these miniseries represent television at its best throughout the 2010s.

A spiritual sequel to their 2001 masterpiece Band of Brothers, The Pacific sees Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks again taking small-screen drama to the front lines of WWII with an immersion into the Pacific Theater of the war that is as grueling as it is gripping. Following the experiences of three American soldiers from different regiments, the miniseries examines the chaos and carnage of the campaign, depicting battles such as Iwo Jima, Okinawa, and Guadalcanal.

Industry observers note that earning universal acclaim for its visceral authenticity, The Pacific is a brutal masterpiece of war drama that soars on the back of its enormous production and the impact of its performances. Enriched by its endeavor to go beyond the ordeal of battle and explore the impact the war had on soldiers returning home, The Pacific is a contemplative and considered examination of those involved in the war. This breathtaking miniseries stands as yet another classic foray into the genre from Hanks and Spielberg.

At face value, 2011 was one of the weaker years of the decade for miniseries magnificence. However, it still contains some underappreciated gems, with Mildred Pierce serving as an overlooked drama defined by its adherence to its source material and a litany of powerful performances. The HBO-produced miniseries stars Kate Winslet as Mildred Pierce, a self-sacrificing single mother during the Great Depression who faces hardship as she tries to open a restaurant while striving to win the love and respect of her narcissistic eldest daughter.

Soaring off the back of Winslet’s Emmy Award-winning performance, Mildred Pierce finds an understated impact as a heartbreaking drama of love and desperation that is beautifully acted and delicately written. While some may argue its five-episode run is extensive and results in a number of lulls throughout the miniseries, Mildred Pierce emerges triumphant as one of 2011’s best small-screen offerings. This period piece immerses audiences in the rigors of Depression-era America and the many obstacles a single mother faced in such a time.

Industry observers note that A three-part romantic drama exploring the impact the AIDS epidemic of the 1980s had on Stockholm’s gay community, Don’t Ever Wipe Tears Without Gloves excels with its artful presentation and delicate handling of its characters and their turmoil. Over the miniseries' three episodes, titled “Love,” “Diseases,” and “Death,” the miniseries follows 19-year-old Rasmus (Adam Pålsson) as he seeks out Stockholm’s gay community and begins a relationship with Benjamin (Adam Lundgren) after moving to the city from his rural home to attend university.

The series’ progression, including flashbacks to Rasmus’ childhood and flashforwards to his agonizing final days, is handled respectfully. The story is realized with a quiet visual beauty and powerful use of symbolism that both support the central story of Rasmus and Ben coming to terms with a damning AIDS diagnosis and illustrate the widespread fear and ignorance surrounding the disease at the time. Also incorporating how religious institutions responded to the disease and those suffering from it, Don’t Ever Wipe Tears Without Gloves is a powerful and profoundly human examination of a dark chapter in history marred by speculative terror and homophobia.

Another three-part miniseries from Europe, Generation War is a German WWII drama following the isolated experiences of five friends throughout the conflict. A tale of disillusionment, desperation, and violence, its focus on two soldiers, a nurse, an aspiring singer, and a Jewish man trying to flee the country is bolstered by its analysis of the corruption of totalitarianism. It doesn’t shirk the fact that a lot of Germans were in favor of Adolf Hitler’s vision of the world, only to be confronted with the hardship of surviving it.

While it has flaws, Generation War is defined by its striking maturity and ability to find sympathy in its main characters through their youthful naivety and brutal disenchantment. Its inherent appeals for forgiveness for those who felt helplessly complicit in the Nazi agenda may be misguided at times. However, the series showcases in unflinching fashion the harsh reality of war and the punishing final truth that, even for those who emerged from the conflict alive, there was little joy and no glory awaiting them at the end of the war.

Sources indicate that starring Frances McDormand and featuring an all-star supporting cast that includes Richard Jenkins, Jesse Plemons, Rachel Brosnahan, and Bill Murray, among others, Olive Kitteridge is a sorrowful, sweeping drama firmly focused on human connection. Based on Elizabeth Strout’s 2008 novel of the same name, the four-episode miniseries follows the titular Kitteridge, a retired schoolteacher with a misanthropic edge and underlying depression, and her strained familial relationships as they unfold over 25 years.

Recent findings suggest that the narrative runs at a slow and measured pace. In this meticulous tempo, the performances of the actors and the impact of the writing flourish, delivering a grounded drama that makes an impression through its sincerity and tenderness. At once bleak and uplifting, Olive Kitteridge is always compelling, delving into the minutiae of life’s complexity with an enticing character who, while sympathetic, is often the source of her problems.

Industry observers note that adapted from Agatha Christie’s novel of the same name, And Then There Were None is something of an underrated gem of 2010s mystery television. Constantly intriguing with its notions of justice and punishment, it follows eight individuals as they converge on the isolated Soldier Island by invitation of a “Mr. and Mrs. Owen,” where they are seen by the island house’s caretakers. When one of the guests is killed, the others learn that they are ensnared in an elaborate ruse: each of them is responsible for an unjust death, and the killer—who is among them—has no intention of stopping until all of them are dead.

It has been revealed that as dashing as it is dark, the miniseries thrives on the talent of its ensemble cast and the misanthropic lens with which it views its characters. Loyal in plot and spirit to Christie’s 1939 novel, And Then There Were None offers intoxicating suspense and intrigue as it marries its psychological murder-mystery antics with an impressive rogues' gallery of amoral and corrupt characters.

According to recent reports, an eight-part miniseries defined by its constant and weighted sense of tension and the impact of its performances, The Night Of is one of HBO’s defining triumphs in the wheelhouse of limited series entertainment. It follows Nasir (Riz Ahmed), an American-Pakistani college student accused of murdering a girl he hooked up with at a party. Amid the apparent hopelessness of his case, Nasir forms a bond with an inmate at Rikers Island, while public defender John Stone (John Turturro) represents "Naz", believing there is more to the murder case.

Thriving not only as a gripping murder mystery, but as a dramatic observation of the legal system rife with political overtones and a commentary on racism in America as well, The Night Of excels through its timely notes of social criticism as much as it does through its captivating suspense. It's further enriched by a detailed mystery that methodically unfolds and Nasir’s surprising coming-of-age story that unfurls behind bars. The miniseries is loaded with intrigue and interest that make it one of the more noteworthy efforts of the decade.

One of the best Western stories to have graced the screen in recent years, Godless excels as a typically violent and vivacious take on the genre that challenges its male-dominated history with a brilliantly conceived story that allows for a mostly female cast. The town of La Belle, populated almost exclusively by women after a mining accident killed most of the men, becomes the center of an outlaw’s vengeance when his prodigy, Roy Goode (Jack O’Connell), seeks refuge, having split off from his gang with a stash of money.

The story takes a keen interest not only in Goode’s relationship with widowed rancher Alice Fletcher (Michelle Dockery), but also in several other figures within the town and the unique struggles they endure. Netflix's Godless is defined by its scope and ambition as well as its smart subversion of Western conventions. A confident piece of genre deconstruction that is often pulsating and quite tender when it needs to be, the Netflix original series tackles femininity in the Old West with compelling grit and refreshing insight to be a true highlight of 2010s television.

It has been revealed that one of the most shocking series of any genre of the 2010s, Sharp Objects finds a compelling depth and striking unpredictability in its basis on Gillian Flynn’s debut novel of the same name. Amy Adams stars as Camille Preaker, a crime reporter who, after being released from a psychiatric hospital after battling alcoholism and depression, returns to her hometown to investigate the murders of two young girls. The disturbing nature of the case clashes with Camille’s strained relationships with her family, forcing her to confront her demons.

Bolstered by an array of exceptional performances, Sharp Objects is a true slow-burn tale that extracts every ounce of tension and drama from its story, entrancing viewers in the immersive allure of its bleak atmosphere rife with moments of agonizing suspense. Bereft of cat-and-mouse chaos or the tantalizing menace of a criminal mastermind, the series instead demands a typically brilliant turn from Adams to explore the full breadth of Camille’s internal struggles with deft drama and nuance. Unsurprisingly, the actress delivers in spades, compelling viewers for the entirety of the series’ eight-episode run and right up to its shocking climax.

Industry observers note that A true masterpiece of small-screen drama, Chernobyl is comfortably among the greatest miniseries of all time and saw the 2010s end in spectacular fashion from the perspective of television entertainment. The precise, procedural historical drama transpires in the aftermath of the Chernobyl nuclear plant disaster of 1986, focusing on the immediate clean-up efforts, the fear that the radiation emitted could impact most of mainland Europe, and the eventual trial to determine culpability for the avoidable catastrophe.

Realized with near-unbearable tension, the series thrives with its imposing scope. It runs as an all-encompassing dramatization of the many sacrificial acts that ensured the disaster didn’t exacerbate, and the political conniving that tried to conceal the truth for as long as possible. It is a masterpiece of creeping dread, an eye-opening display of real-world institutional corrosion, and one of the most absorbingly horrific stories that has ever been put to screen. It will endure as an important masterwork for many years to come.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains minor spoilers for "Focker In-Law.".

Recent findings suggest that although it's not the only way comedy sequels can be successful, whether or not they stand out often comes down to their jokes. After all, while most of the great comedy sequels earn their status by being just as much or nearly as unique as their predecessors, if the jokes are lacking, then it's all for naught. This is why many comedy sequels are identified not by their character arcs or plot but by their gags and setpieces. "Gremlins 2: The Latest Batch" will primarily be known for its inclusion of wilder and weirder Gremlins, "Addams Family Values" has a memorable Thanksgiving play sequence, and so on.

Industry observers note that so far, the "Meet the Parents" franchise has enjoyed its longevity thanks to adding new stars to the Focker family and beyond. "Meet the Fockers" introduced Barbara Streisand and Dustin Hoffman as the parents of Ben Stiller's Greg Focker, while "Little Fockers" used the occasion of the Fockers having babies to include new faces such as Jessica Alba's Andi. This month's "Focker In-Law" continues the tradition by casting hot young talents Skyler Gisondo and Beanie Feldstein as the Focker children, with Ariana Grande also turning up in a major role as Greg's son's fiancé. However, writer/director John Hamburg cleverly understood that he couldn't solely rely on the cast to make his film stand out. He wanted to conceive a sequence that would match the cringe comedy outrageousness of the original film while using all his stars in a substantial way. He does so in the moment where Greg sings John Legend's "All of Me" to Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro), which, according to Hamburg himself, is the best scene in the movie.

Sources indicate that one of the things "Focker In-Law" does really well is escalation, in which Greg Focker makes a series of choices which have minor consequences at first but quickly snowball into increasingly more ludicrous events. The apex of this is when Greg (Ben Stiller), who has taken it upon himself to keep Henry (Skyler Gisondo) from proposing to Olivia (Ariana Grande) by hiding the engagement ring, discovers at the last minute that Henry had secretly planned to sing a song at dinner with everyone present. Scrambling, Greg decides to perform the song himself, and dedicate it to his occasional family nemesis, Jack.

According to recent reports, when I had the opportunity to speak to Hamburg about the movie, he chose this setpiece as the best scene in the film from a subjective and objective perspective. As he explained:.

"I'd say for this movie, it's recency bias, but there's a scene where Greg serenades Jack. And most of the cast is sitting around this table and Owen Wilson's at the piano. And that was just a really epic moment in my career as a filmmaker. To have these amazingly talented people gathered on one set and then have Ben singing and Bob's reactions are so priceless. It was just like everything kind of came together. That's like the dream for a comedy filmmaker, to have that. And then the audience reaction was so great. [...] There's many [great scenes], but of many, I'd say that sequence is one I reflect on. It's like, that was a really fun couple of days of shooting.".

It has been revealed that given how well it works both in and out of context, the scene is absolutely a standout moment. And who knows, maybe Stiller will sing again in the next "Focker" film because of it.

"Focker In-Law" is in theaters now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sandwiched between the kitschy horrors of Halloween and the commercialized merriment of Christmas, Thanksgiving is often unfairly overlooked as a cinematic main course. But while there might not be a feast’s worth of Thanksgiving movies, there is undoubtedly an appetite for Thanksgiving fare in film. Look no further than the inclusion of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in Miracle on 34th Street or Wednesday Adams’s sinister (if historically-accurate) re-enactment in Addams Family Values for proof that audiences love turkey’s least favorite holiday. Of course, Thanksgiving tends to get a better treatment on TV, inspiring canonical episodes of Gossip Girl, Friends, Master of None, and, of course, A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving.

Nevertheless, we’ve collected 21 Thanksgiving movies (and Thanksgiving-adjacent movies) that capture the spirit of the holiday—turkey-trotting, tossing the pigskin, carb-loading, fighting with your family, and then overheating in a gorgeous cashmere sweater. Here’s to finding post-meal common ground with one of the titles on this list.

Sources indicate that this isn’t known as the quintessential Thanksgiving movie for nothing. You know the story: Steve Martin’s uptight marketing executive, Neal, just wants to travel from Newly introduced York to Chicago for turkey with his family. His plans for an uneventful trip are foiled again and again by John Candy’s boisterous shower-ring salesman, Del, who’s eager to make friends with Neal during their wayward journey. We will never look at pillows—or rental car agents—the same way again.

Don’t let the word Christmas in the title scare you away. This 2016 ensemble comedy starring Danny Glover, Kimberly Elise, Mo’Nique, and Gabrielle Union has undeniable Thanksgiving vibes. Produced by Will Packer and originally sold to Universal Pictures under the title A Meyers Thanksgiving, Almost Christmas follows the dysfunctional Meyers family as the family patriarch, Walter Meyers (Glover), tries to get through his first holiday season after the death of his wife. While it isn’t exactly about Thanksgiving per se, most of the best moments in Almost Christmas—including Elise chasing Romany Malco away from the table with a shotgun, or the whole table having to pretend to like Mo’Nique’s terrible food—take place during large family gatherings around the dinner table. What could be more Thanksgiving-coded than that? With an all-star cast of Black actors that also includes J.B. Smoove, Nicole Ari Parker, Omar Epps, and Gladys Knight, Almost Christmas feels like a homecoming full of your favorite uncles and aunties. And, to be fair, isn’t Thanksgiving almost Christmas?

It has been revealed that the turkey isn’t the only thing getting carved up in this holiday slasher. Starring Patrick Dempsey and Tik Toker turned recording artist turned film actress Addison Rae, Thanksgiving begins with a Black Friday sale gone horribly awry in Plymouth, Massachusetts, leading to the death of multiple customers. The following year, a murderous slasher wearing a John Carver mask is wreaking havoc in Plymouth, and targeting Rae’s Gaby and her friends. If you’re not feeling warm and gooey on over the holiday, you might want to throw on Thanksgiving and watch Rae and Dempsey’s Sheriff Eric Newton try and track down and escape the clutches of a grisly murderer.

In Jodie Foster’s comedy, Holly Hunter plays Claudia Larson, who returns home for Thanksgiving after losing her job and learning that her daughter (My So-Called Life–era Claire Danes) intends to spend the holiday with a boyfriend. The family she returns to is filled with colorful performances from Anne Bancroft and Charles Durning as her eclectic parents, Robert Downey Jr. as her misanthrope brother, and Dylan McDermott as a semi-mysterious dinner guest.

Fantastic Mr. Fox isn’t technically about Thanksgiving, or even really about humans. And yet, Wes Anderson’s 2009 stop-motion film, featuring the voices of George Clooney and Meryl Streep, has been labeled a Thanksgiving must-watch. Perhaps that’s because the film, based on Roald Dahl’s classic children’s novel, is all about animals trying to escape the tyranny of farmers—something every turkey not lucky enough to be pardoned by the president wishes it could do around Thanksgiving time. Beyond the war between animals and farmers, Anderson’s rustic color palette filled with burnt orange—and the massive feast that brings a diverse array of animals around a dinner table after they successfully joined forces to steal food from their nemeses—are full of the spirit of Thanksgiving.

In a recent development, at times, the titular April’s (Katie Holmes) fate feels as if it rests on whether she’ll successfully cook a turkey in her crowded Lower East Side apartment. As April prepares to host her suburban Pennsylvania family, the high-stakes nature of spending a day hunkered down with relatives—played by Patricia Clarkson, Oliver Platt, Alison Pill, and John Gallagher Jr.—rushes in.

In a recent development, sometimes getting families together over the holidays is fraught. In this 1997 moody drama directed by Ang Lee, two affluent Connecticut families unravel over Thanksgiving break as their secrets come to lights. The ensemble cast includes stalwart actors Kevin Kline, Joan Allen, Sigourney Weaver as messy parents, and, at that point, up and comers, Tobey Maguire, Elijah Wood, and Christina Ricci as their even more troubled teens. The Ice Storm, which won best screenplay at Cannes Film Festival, is rife with adultery, substance abuse, as well as surprising turns from a host of talented actors and a sharp early film from one of cinema’s most celebrated directors.

Nothing feels more nostalgic during Thanksgiving than watching Snoopy whip up a makeshift meal with jelly beans, popcorn, and mountains of buttered toast for all of his Peanuts pals. And Vince Guraldi’s timeless score makes for a perfect soundtrack to your own festivities.

A Thanksgiving flashback provides key context for the complicated dynamics amongst this group of recently-reunited college friends, played by Glenn Close, Kevin Kline, Jeff Goldblum, Mary Kay Place, and William Hurt. Lawrence Kasdan’s film earned three Oscar nominations, including best picture, original screenplay, and supporting actress for Close.

While not a Thanksgiving-themed film, protagonist Nola Darling (Tracy Camilla Johns) invites all three of her potential suitors to a tense dinner on that very holiday, making her memorable decision between them from her head-of-the-table vantage point. This was most of the world’s introduction to Spike Lee, both as an actor and director, and the electricity is still palpable. And if you’ve gotta have more? You can always stream the 2017 Netflix original series of the same name, starring Lee and DeWanda Wise as Nola Darling.

Rian Johnson’s whodunnit has all the trappings of a Thanksgiving movie, without ever mentioning the holiday. There’s family infighting, Chris Evans in a cable-knit sweater, foggy fall weather, and even a political allegory about the treatment of people of color. Also not about Thanksgiving, but worthy viewing for the full family: Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery, which hit theaters last November.

The same year that Merriam-Webster acknowledged Instagram captions everywhere by adding “Friendsgiving” to the dictionary, a movie of the same name was released. True to its titular tradition, a group of friends convenes for a meal that inevitably devolves into chaos.

According to recent reports, while not an outright Thanksgiving movie, 1997’s ensemble dramedy contains some of the most sumptuous shots of food ever committed to film. After the death of their family matriarch, a group of disparate relatives must put aside their differences and reconvene for a weekly Sunday dinner. Starring Vivica A. Fox, Vanessa Williams, and Nia Long, Soul Food captures the bonding powers that plates of cornbread, catfish, and collard greens can bring.

It has been revealed that this 1976 best picture Oscar winner stars Sylvester Stallone as the eponymous down-on-his-luck boxer, whose fate begins to change with the meeting of his future wife, Adrian (Talia Shire). “To you, it’s Thanksgiving. To me, it’s Thursday,” Rocky tells Adrian as he whisks her away from a disastrous family feast minutes after her brother Paulie (Burt Young) hurls her turkey into the nearby alley. As fans of the franchise, which has debuted several films over the Thanksgiving holiday, know, their Thanksgiving meet-cute will stand the test of time.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving isn’t always about bickering with your blood relatives. Spend Thanksgiving with Instant Family, which stars Mark Wahlberg and Rose Byrne as Pete and Ellie Wagner, an unwitting couple who, overnight, become parents to three foster children. Their decision to become parents happens over  a tense Thanksgiving dinner where Ellie’s family shares they don’t think that Pete and Ellie were ever really cut out to be parents. In an effort to prove them wrong, the Wagners wind up biting off more than they bargained for as they become foster parents to three children, the eldest played by Madame Web star Isabela Merced.

Before Greta Gerwig forced Noah Baumbach to write Barbie with her, there was Mistress America. Written by the real-life couple who helmed the billion dollar blockbuster, this 2015 Sundance favorite centers on the unlikely friendship between Lola Kirke’s Tracy, a first-year college student alone in New York, and Gerwig’s Brooke, the Times Square-living twentysomething who will soon become her stepsister. Conflict between the pair gets resolved on Thanksgiving at New York City’s Veselka, a Ukrainian institution where pierogis stand in for the traditional bird.

Sources indicate that greta Gerwig must really love Thanksgiving. The auteur’s Oscar-nominated take on the Louisa May Alcott classic is brimming with cozy, Thanksgiving-esque vibes. Set largely in the weeks before Christmas, the March sisters (Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Eliza Scanlen, and Florence Pugh) and matriarch (Laura Dern) battle wits, trot through the snow, and stage living room plays in a film that feels reminiscent of many a-family gatherings.

“First, let’s give thanks to our families not being here. It’s always easier without the family,” Adam Sandler’s George Simmons, a stand-up comedian who has been newly diagnosed with cancer, says to a group of new friends. In Judd Apatow’s 2009 dramedy, George attempts to revamp his fledgling career in the eleventh hour with the help of aspiring comic Ira Wright (Seth Rogen). At one point, he  joins the younger talent’s friendsgiving festivities, where the table is surrounded by stars including Jonah Hill, Jason Schwartzman, Aubrey Plaza, and Bo Burnham.

It has been revealed that in one of the newer entries to the turkey day canon, Stephen Karam adapts his 2015 Pulitzer finalist play of the same name, exploring the long-held resentments and deeply-rooted admiration that live in an East Coast family. Jayne Houdyshell reprises her Tony-winning role as Deirdre alongside a stacked ensemble, including Richard Jenkins, June Squibb, Beanie Feldstein, Steven Yeun, and Amy Schumer, all gathered in a drab Chinatown apartment for Thanksgiving.

It has been revealed that prisoners finds Hugh Jackman and Jake Gyllenhaal teaming up to find a pair of missing girls who were abducted after Thanksgiving dinner in Conyers, Pennsylvania. EGOT recipient Viola Davis also stars in the thriller as the mother of one of the kidnapped girls. Directed by Dune’s Denis Villeneuve, Prisoners is an unconventional and unsettling Thanksgiving film.

Another unconventional choice, Sam Raimi’s Spider-Man is arguably the only superhero movie that doubles as a Thanksgiving movie. While the central action follows Tobey Maguire’s Peter Parker, there’s a pivotal scene set at Thanksgiving dinner that directly follows a heated battle between Spider-Man and the Green Goblin (a.k.a Norman Osborne, played by Willem Dafoe.) Parker and Osborne have Thanksgiving dinner together with MJ (Kirsten Dunst), Harry Osborne (James Franco), and Aunt May (Rosemary Harris). During the meal, Osborne comes to the stunning realization that Peter Parker is, in fact, Spider-Man. Others have already made the case that the first Spider-Man film deserves to be included in the Thanksgiving canon. The way Dafoe carves the turkey is also both sinister and iconic, as is Maguire apologizing for his tardiness because he “had to beat an old lady with a stick to get these cranberries.”.
