  • The epic World War II film Battle of the Bulge dramatizes Nazi Germany’s final major Western Front counteroffensive in the Ardennes forest during the winter of 1944.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘Tis the season to be jolly! But while we all celebrate the holidays with our loved ones, we often forget that the world revolves around them. So, at certain moments in world history, wars broke out during Christmas. What did it mean for the men and women on the battlefield? Well, these ten Christmas war movies may offer some insight!

It has been revealed that the ten films use Christmas as a backdrop in a variety of ways, yet they all center around the hardships of battle. From classic films of Hollywood’s Golden Age to newer dramas, these Christmas films may be perfect additions to your holiday rotation. Whether you typically seek out war films or not, the Christmas element may entice you.

The epic World War II film Battle of the Bulge dramatizes Nazi Germany’s final major Western Front counteroffensive in the Ardennes forest during the winter of 1944. As German panzer forces led by Colonel Martin Hessler (Robert Shaw) launch a surprise attack to capture Antwerp, an American intelligence officer named Lieutenant Colonel Daniel Kiley (Henry Fonda) deduces that the advancing enemy tanks will soon run out of fuel and races to stop them from seizing a massive Allied supply depot. Directed by Ken Annakin, Battle of the Bulge works as a holiday film because it presents a Christmas-season WWII setting with a large-scale 1960s roadshow war spectacle known for its tank action sequences, widescreen photography, and strong ensemble cast.

It has been revealed that shot in Ultra Panavision 70 and shown in Cinerama, Battle of the Bulge delivers sweeping armored clashes and memorable set pieces like the tank crews singing "Panzerlied.” Taking historical liberties, the film compresses the campaign and alters terrain and weather, yet presents combat as a heavy, imposing presence. That remarked, the Christmas backdrop comes in as the Ardennes offensive ran across the Christmas and Fresh Year's holidays in 1944, giving the story a grim seasonal contrast. Benjamin Frankel's score weaves carol motifs, such as "Good King Wenceslas" and "The First Noel,” alongside dramatic battle themes. With stellar star power and poignant human moments trickling in between the battle scenes, the film is an easy marriage of holiday setting and epic war story.

It has been revealed that written and directed by Carl Foreman in a piece he deemed a “personal statement,” The Victors is a gritty, episodic anti-war drama that follows an American infantry squad across Europe during World War II, from Britain and Sicily to France and occupied Berlin. Intercutting fictional vignettes with real wartime newsreels, the film explores the dehumanizing psychological toll of combat and the harsh encounters soldiers share with European civilians, illustrating that war leaves no true winners. While its reception upon release was sharply divided, many contemporary viewers and rediscoveries value its bleak realism, ambitious structure, and early shift toward gritty 1960s filmmaking. Its holiday highlight comes in through a haunting holiday sequence that contrasts festive cheer against the brutal reality of combat.

In a recent development, adapted from Alexander Baron's The Human Kind, the film was ahead of its time in its darker tone compared with many wartime spectacles of the era. It rejects conventional battle-glorification in favor of moral disillusionment and historical irony. Foreman stages a harrowing firing-squad execution in a snow-covered setting during the holiday season, modeled on the real-life execution of Private Eddie Slovik. It features an ironic holiday soundtrack as Frank Sinatra’s recording of "Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas" plays against the grim imagery, sharpening the emotional shock rather than offering warm holiday comfort. Rather than cozy sentimentality, the film highlights the harsh conditions endured by soldiers and civilians, giving viewers a sobering reminder of peacetime comforts during the holidays. With a brilliant ensemble featuring George Peppard, George Hamilton, Eli Wallach, Albert Finney, Peter Fonda, Jeanne Moreau, Melina Mercouri, and Romy Schneider, the anthology-style storytelling is worth experiencing the reality of war. ​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that in the Canadian TV film Silent Night, it loosely tells the true story of German mother named Elisabeth Vincken (Linda Hamilton) and her young son Fritz (Matthew Harbour) as they take refuge in a remote Ardennes forest cabin on Christmas Eve 1944. When three lost American soldiers—one severely wounded—and three German soldiers arrive seeking shelter from the winter storm, Elisabeth convinces both sides to leave their weapons outside and share a peaceful holiday meal. Directed by Rodney Gibbons, Silent Night is a heartfelt retelling of a World War II truce that is grounded in humanity. It turns an intimate Christmas Eve moment and turns it into a character-driven story of hope.

Silent Night is a special film. Rather than relying on large-scale battle spectacle, the intimate cabin setting highlights the contrast between Christmas warmth and war's harshness. Choosing humanity over stereotypes, the soldiers share rations and a holiday meal; initial hostility gives way to shared vulnerability and common ground across enemy lines. Having armed enemies share tight quarters, after agreeing to leave weapons outside, creates genuine suspense and forced empathy. Familiar Christmas traditions like sharing food, trimming a tree, and singing carols collide with grief, fear, and wartime loyalties. Moments of camaraderie stay fragile rather than turning into easy sentimentality. Hamilton stands out, playing Elisabeth with quiet authority and moral clarity, refusing to let hatred or war dictate what happens under her roof. Silent Night takes a true story and does it justice. ​​​​​​​.

While it may not have a direct holiday plotline, Where Eagles Dare gets lumped into the holiday war viewing for its Boxing Day debut and its snow-covered alpine setting. Directed by Brian G. Hutton, the epic action-adventure film set during World War II follows British Major John Smith (Richard Burton) and American Lieutenant Morris Schaffer (Clint Eastwood) as they lead an elite commando unit disguised as German soldiers into the Bavarian Alps to rescue a captured U.S. general holding D-Day invasion looks from an impregnable mountain fortress. As the team infiltrates the castle, they uncover a web of double-crosses and traitors within their own ranks, turning a straightforward rescue into a deadly espionage trap. Where Eagles Dare emerged as a classic, blending high-stakes World War II espionage with relentless, practical action and memorable star power.

Written by Alistair MacLean, the story blends a castle-infiltration rescue mission with constant double-crosses and shifting loyalties that keep viewers guessing. Filming on location in Austria and Bavaria, including sequences atop moving cable cars in harsh winter weather, gives the action a visceral weight. With a winter wonderland backdrop, the film receives a fairytale-fortress feel amid blizzards and freezing cold. Burton brings theatrical intensity as Major John Smith while Eastwood plays Lieutenant Morris Schaffer with sharp efficiency. Their pairing creates sharp dramatic friction as the mission escalates. Where Eagles Dare is a sweeping, larger-than-life classic that deserves a watch when a chill fills the air. ​​​​​​​.

Directed by Nagisa Ōshima from a screenplay by Ōshima and Paul Mayersberg, the holiday-tinged war film Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence is set in a 1942 Japanese prisoner-of-war camp on Java. The film explores the intense cultural and psychological clash between British captives and their strict Japanese captors during World War II. As rebellious British Major Jack Celliers (David Bowie) sparks a tense battle of wills and mutual fascination with camp commander Captain Yonoi (Ryuichi Sakamoto), fluent Japanese-speaking officer Lt. Col. John Lawrence (Tom Conti) works to bridge their divide and prevent bloodshed. Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence turns a World War II prisoner-of-war story into an intimate psychological study of clashing cultures, honor, and unspoken desire. The film subverts both holiday sentimentality and traditional combat tropes, choosing character over battle.

In a recent development, merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence explores how rigid military codes and personal guilt shape human connection. Strict Bushido ideals and camp commandant Captain Yonoi's rigid discipline collide with Major Jack Celliers's defiant spirit and Lieutenant Colonel John Lawrence's role as a cultural bridge. Rather than treating captors and prisoners as simple caricatures, the film explores obsession, guilt, and shifting loyalties. Instead of cozy holiday cheer, Christmas arrives amid harsh POW camp conditions, heightening the contrast between seasonal goodwill and wartime cruelty. Its wintry, melancholic mood pairs well with late-year reflection, anchored by themes of forgiveness, memory, and survival. Bowie is absolutely magnetic, bringing distinct intensity and vulnerability. With an emotionally fueled score and its lush, sometimes surreal visuals paired with tense quietness, Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence may not excuse holiday tidings, but it hammers home the power of connection. ​​​​​​​.

Sources indicate that one of the greatest war stories ever told is the subject of the Christian Carion film Joyeux Noël. Inspired by the real-life Christmas Truce of 1914, the World War I film follows French, Scottish, and German soldiers on the Western Front who spontaneously lay down their weapons on Christmas Eve to sing carols, share gifts, and play soccer in No Man's Land. As opposing troops bond over their shared humanity, they must eventually confront the harsh disapproval of their military superiors once the fleeting ceasefire ends. Joyeux Noël is a remarkable piece for its emotional impact, international ensemble cast, and poignant depiction of Christmas on the Western Front.

It has been revealed that earning an Academy Award nomination for Best Foreign Language Film, Joyeux Noël is a joyous production. Told through multi-language realism, the film reinforces the cross-border camaraderie and cultural friction of the front lines. Joyeux Noël pairs the brutality of World War I trench warfare with the genuine warmth, music, and shared humanity. Music plays a central role, as a Scottish bagpiper and a German opera tenor help spark the ceasefire with familiar holiday songs like "Silent Night" and "Adeste Fideles," turning the battlefield into common ground. Paired with Philippe Rombi's score and snowy winter cinematography, the film sparks the holiday spirit with goodwill front and center. It’s a greeting card-quality film. Rather than ending on a purely fairy-tale note, the story indicates the harsh military repercussions soldiers face afterward for fraternizing with the enemy. ​​​​​​​.

In this depiction of the Battle of the Bulge, Battleground director William A. Wellman tells the story of a squad of U.S. Army soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division trapped by German forces in Bastogne, Belgium, during the December 1944 Battle of the Bulge. Cut off from supplies and air support by thick winter fog, the exhausted men battle freezing temperatures, dwindling rations, and disguised enemy infiltrators as they fight to survive until Allied reinforcements can break the siege. The Academy Award-winning war film strips away wartime heroics and grand speeches to show the gritty, everyday reality of American soldiers trapped in Bastogne during the Battle of the Bulge. The film pairs a snowy winter atmosphere and a Christmas Eve service with a grounded portrait of endurance and camaraderie.

Instead of turning the men of the 101st Airborne into larger-than-life icons, screenwriter Robert Pirosh, a veteran of the battle, focuses on fear, fatigue, griping, and moments of doubt. Characters complain, slack off, or briefly consider running away, making their eventual endurance and camaraderie feel earned rather than inevitable. The film relies on an ensemble cast, including Van Johnson, John Hodiak, Ricardo Montalbán, George Murphy, and Oscar-nominated James Whitmore, working as a unit rather than centering on a single star. Christmas Eve in the line serves as a monumental moment in the film. A chaplain holds a Christmas service for the men, framing why the fight against fascism is necessary while soldiers face overwhelming odds and German surrender demands. Once the weather clears enough for planes to reach the trapped troops, supply drops of food, fuel, and ammunition act like hard-won holiday gifts. Battleground is an unvarnished story with dark humor, stark black-and-white winter visuals, and genuine realism. ​​​​​​​.

Set in snowy Ardennes Forest in December 1944, A Midnight Clear, written and directed by Keith Gordon, follows a depleted six-man American intelligence squad stationed at an isolated French chateau as they encounter a weary German platoon that wants to surrender rather than fight in Germany's final offensive. After sharing an unexpected Christmas truce with their enemies, the young soldiers arrange a staged skirmish, so the Germans can safely surrender without being branded traitors, only for a tragic misunderstanding to turn their peaceful blueprint deadly. A Midnight Clear trades typical combat action for a quiet, character-driven study of isolation, morality, and absurdity during World War II. Adapted from William Wharton's novel, the film stands out as a great Christmas film, using the holiday's quiet, reflective spirit to capture the grim emotional toll of World War II.

Christmas carols, a makeshift tree, and a snowball fight contrast sharply with winter cold, psychological weight, and the grim realities of conflict. Snow-covered woods, isolated estates, and eerie quiet give the film a fairy-tale, almost surreal tone. Despite the war backdrop, the winter setting underscores isolation and fragility. The film refuses easy sentimentality. Its tragic turn reminds viewers how fragile peace is when war's machinery is still running. The film features strong, grounded performances from Ethan Hawke, Gary Sinise, Kevin Dillon, Arye Gross, Peter Berg, Frank Whaley, and John C. McGinley. Rather than relying on grand heroics, the cast captures young men dealing with fear, fatigue, and unspoken strain. A Midnight Clear has the DNA of a war saga, but its haunting winter atmosphere turns it into something grander. ​​​​​​​.

Directed by John Cromwell, the 1944 war epic Since You Went Away follows Anne Hilton (Claudette Colbert) and her two daughters, Jane and Bridget (Jennifer Jones and Shirley Temple), as they navigate rationing, romance, and personal sacrifices on the American home front after her husband leaves for World War II. Joined by a retired colonel and loyal household staff, the family endures wartime heartbreak and uncertainty before receiving hopeful news on Christmas Eve. Since You Went Away is a moving portrayal of World War II home-front life. With a deeply emotional Christmas Eve payoff, Since You Went Away is a perfect Yuletide classic to share with the family.

Industry observers note that unlike war films centered on combat, this home-front classic focuses on individuals as they navigate rationing, separation, and everyday worries at home. It captures the longing, resilience, and hope of families waiting for loved ones to return that resonates with a timeless sentiment for any wartime family. Rather than focusing on the battlefield, the emotional power stems from daily life in America, where ration books, victory gardens, housing shortages, scrap drives, and civilian sacrifice were a reality. The story balances lighthearted moments, like a hangar dance and teenage romance, with gut-wrenching goodbyes, including Jane and Bill Smollett’s (Robert Walker) famous midnight train station parting. Since You Went Away may be the most sentimental Christmas-based war film of all time. ​​​​​​​.

Blending dark comedy and suspenseful mystery inside a World War II prisoner-of-war camp, Stalag 17 is a brilliant feature. Directed by Billy Wilder, the story follows barracks of American airmen who suspect a cynical, black-marketeering sergeant named J.J. Sefton (William Holden) of being a Nazi informant after two escaping prisoners are killed. Determined to clear his name, Sefton investigates the barracks to expose the real German spy and orchestrate a daring escape. Stalag 17 balances broad barracks humor and gallows comedy with genuine paranoia and suspense as American airmen hunt for a German spy among them. Set during Christmas week in 1944, the holiday becomes a source of brilliant irony.

Industry observers note that between Wilder's direction and Holden's Oscar-winning lead performance, Stalag 17 is simply wonderful. The tension comes from paranoia inside Barracks 4 as American airmen try to figure out who is leaking escape prepares. The film builds suspense to an epic reveal set to "When Johnny Comes Marching Home,” earning it an iconic moment in the genre and a blueprint for directing tension. As for the Christmas backdrop, makeshift decorations, dog-tag trees, and a camp Christmas party clash with the harsh reality of captivity and fatal escape attempts. Camp commandant Colonel von Scherbach (Otto Preminger) even plays a cruel parody of holiday generosity around an inspection. The film celebrates bittersweet camaraderie in moments like when the men dance together during the holiday celebration and Stanislas "Animal" Kuzawa’s (Robert Strauss) poignant mix of slapstick and loneliness. They highlight brotherhood and longing for home without turning overtly sentimental. Adapted from the Broadway play by former POWs Donald Bevan and Edmund Trzcinski, the film treats captivity with a realistic edge rather than pure escapism. It even shaped later television comedies like Hogan's Heroes.

‘Filipiñana’ Could Be the Philippines’ First-Ever Oscar-Shortlisted Feature — Even as the Film Was Dealt an Unexpected Tragedy

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A posh, Philippine country club’s colonial secrets are exposed in Rafael Manuel’s evocatively creepy, grimly funny, and austerely constructed social satire, “Filipiñana,” set outside Manila.

According to recent reports, writer/director Rafael Manuel’s film, which won a World Cinema special jury award at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, also stands a chance at being his country’s first representative on a Best International Feature Film Oscar shortlist. While the Philippines was among the eight countries that submitted during the category’s inaugural year in 1956 (with Lamberto V. Avellana’s “Child of Sorrow”) along with France, Italy, and others, it’s never been nominated or shortlisted. Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’.

Executive-produced by Manuel’s former mentor Jia Zhangke, “Filipiñana” follows a tee girl who discovers something is off (and downright sinister) about the club’s administration, specifically president Dr. Palanca (Teroy Guzman). She’s played by Jorrybell Agoto, who, at just 32 years old, died earlier in November after a short battle with lymphoma.

IndieWire’s interview with filmmaker Rafael Manuel took place a week before the news, though he shared in a later statement, “The tragedy of this loss cannot be put into words. The world has just lost one of its brightest stars. We have just lost a great friend. But our thoughts and prayers go out especially to Jorybell’s family, who have just lost a loving ate [the Filipino word for older sister] and a devoted daughter.”.

An elegaic air, too, hangs over the film in retrospect and even before Agoto’s passing, as “Filipiñana” dwells in ghosts of the Philippines’ imperial past and Spanish occupation.

Industry observers note that “No one explains it to you beforehand,” director Manuel told IndieWire of touring with his first feature for nearly a year. (We spoke over Zoom while he smoked a cigarette in his Amsterdam apartment.) “What I’m starting to realize is the biggest difference between short and feature is that with short festival, it’s kind of the end goal. When you premiere at your festival, you’re so happy, and it’s done; it’s like people get to see it finally. But with a feature film, it’s just the beginning, and no one explained this to me.”.

Manuel joins the ranks of Lav Diaz, Brillante Mendoza, the late Lino Brocka, and many others to represent the Philippines at the Academy Awards — a concept, he noted, that was never really on his radar.

“When we were coming up with this film and the genesis of the film, you don’t really think about an Oscars race,” stated Manuel. “You just think about making the best film you can. And especially coming from Southeast Asia, access to the American market, even getting a U.S. theatrical release, it’s not something that’s very common. Usually, your usual route is via the European arthouse market. So it’s been really surprising and in the best way possible, seeing how well received the film is in the States, in North America, and in the Anglo world in general.”.

In a recent development, the process was a “very challenging one,” he said, as the Philippines is taking the Oscar push very seriously from a governmental perspective. “And to be the first film that’s seriously backed by the government means a lot to us,” he said, especially for a film that’s critical of government and social hierarchy.

And there are hat tips not only to Jacques Tati, but also to Wes Anderson and Michael Haneke, at least in reviews, in terms of the movie’s flattened remove from violence and its dryly observational approach where everything in the frame is meticulously arranged.

“I get why people are saying Michael Haneke and Wes Anderson,” he remarked. “I mean, Jacques Tati, obviously, he’s a really big influence for me, but for example, with Haneke, I feel like we tackle violence very differently from how Haneke tackles violence. And I think with Wes Anderson, I see it because of the colors, because of the symmetrical framing and all of that, but I think this is very much a satire of that. And so, yes, we use a lot of Western codes and Western aesthetics in the film, but because it’s a film that deals with Western influence in the Orient, it was a film that deals with colonization. So the form and the aesthetic of the film is very much part of the satire. It’s the form.”.

It has been revealed that he added, “It’s a polarizing film. I think it’s either you love it or you hate it, and I think that’s the same whether you’re in the West or in the Philippines.”.

The distribution of world cinema in the Philippines also helps to explain the divided palate for “Filipiñana,” as audiences have very little exposure to arthouse cinema from the outside world.

It has been revealed that “In the Philippines, distribution of world cinema, it’s almost nonexistent. In Metro Manila, we have basically one or two arthouse cinemas, independent cinemas. The rest of the cinemas are all in shopping malls, and all they play are local rom-coms or Marvel movies,” he remarked. But issues in the West of audience fatigue over shopworn, recycled I.P. and familiar material also apply in the Philippines.

“It’s been a hot topic lately in the Philippines and consumers and audiences complaining about formulaic Filipino filmmaking. They’re tired of the formulaic rom-coms. But then the thing is that in the Philippines, I would say 90 percent of people have never seen a Lav Diaz film, even maybe 99 percent of people haven’t seen a Lav Diaz film,” Manuel stated of the slow cinema master behind last year’s submission, the Gael García Bernal-starring “Magellan,” which also dealt in the Philippines’ colonized history. (Diaz and Manuel share producers, including Bianca Balbuena and Bradley Liew, though they’ve never actually met.).

“Filipiñana” marks a break from tradition in terms of its Westernized style — and chatter has been flying on Letterboxd over the film since the Sundance premiere. (“I look through Letterboxd sometimes. Well, I used to, I stopped. And then the unhealthy thing with Letterboxd, for me especially, is that I’ll skip all the good comments and I’ll just read all the bad comments,” he said.).

“When you’re faced with something different with arthouse cinema, like Filipino arthouse cinema, when Filipino audiences are faced with Filipino arthouse cinema, and you get some violent reactions, then it begs the question, ‘When you’re complaining about being tired of formulaic Filipino filmmaking, what exactly do you mean, and what exactly is it that you want?’ Do you just want Hollywood films but with brown faces in them? Because I don’t think that’s the answer either.”.

“Filipiñana” is now streaming on Kino Film Collection.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, marvel Comics fans know Doctor Victor von Doom is scarcely ever seen without his iron mask — a mask that hides his supposedly horribly scarred face.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, marvel Comics fans know Doctor Victor von Doom is scarcely ever seen without his iron mask — a mask that hides his supposedly horribly scarred face. But with Marvel Studios choosing former Tony Stark actor Robert Downey Jr. to play Doom in the upcoming "Avengers" movies "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars," there's been an expectation that Doom's mask coming off will be a jaw dropping moment.

Now, Chris Evans has claimed that Doom wears his mask for the entirety of "Doomsday." But that could only mean he'll keep the mask on until "Secret Wars." Even then, there's the chance that Doom is so disfigured that his face isn't even recognizable as RDJ. A new TV spot for "Doomsday" does suggest Doom has his scarred face, while also teasing we're eventually going to see exactly what's under his mask ... but not yet.

In this TV spot, Magneto (Ian McKellen) tries to telekinetically rip off Doom's mask — it is made of metal, after all. But Doom does not restrict himself to the laws of science. There's evidently a magical seal on the mask (note there appear to be runic designs across Doom's costume), because glowing green tendrils extend out from Doom's hood and grab the mask, slamming it back onto Doom's face. A brief glimpse of Doom's face, visible through the mask's eyeholes, shows hints of pale macerated skin and scar tissue.

Recent findings suggest that in the "Fantastic Four" comics, it was originally mentioned that Doom suffered his scars during an experiment in college. A machine he built to contact the "nether world" (later revealed to be an attempt to reach his mother's damned soul) exploded in his face, leaving him scarred.

Now, Doom's co-creator Jack Kirby intended that Doom actually only had a thin facial scar — but Doom's ego can't stand even that small imperfection. Later "Fantastic Four" writer/artist John Byrne melded the two ideas. The machine explosion only slightly damaged Doom's face, but then Victor — convinced his face was already ruined — put his freshly forged mask on before it cooled, and that is why he has a horribly scarred face.

The greatest source of Doom's torment is completely self-inflicted. The exemplary 1989 "Doctor Strange and Doctor Doom: Triumph and Torment" goes with Byrne's interpretation. When Doom seeks out the wisdom of the wizard named the Aged Genghis, the sorcerer alludes to Doom's "minor disfigurement." We then see Doom's (barely scarred) face as Victor lashes out at the insult.

It's unclear what origin "Doomsday" will go with, if any of them. Marketing suggests the Marvel Cinematic Universe's Doom will be driven by a lost wife and child, not his mother. What is clear from this TV spot is that Marvel fans can expect to see Doom and Magneto — the two greatest villains of Marvel Comics — clash onscreen. Doom's wizardry here refutes the obvious conclusion that Magneto wins easily because he controls metal and Doom is concealed inside metal armor.

"He is pain, he is extinction," Magneto declares, setting up Doom's famous third person double entendre: "I am Doom!" Ian McKellen's Magneto was the first villain of the Marvel movie boom that kicked off with 2000's "X-Men." Bringing him back to face (and presumably fall to) Doom is some classic carnival barker marketing that would make Stan Lee proud.

"Avengers: Doomsday" is set for theatrical release on December 18, 2026.

Now, the streamer has added a Christmas-themed romance just in time for the holidays, and this one stars "Landman" actor Michelle Randolph.

The film is called "Clashing Through the Snow" and before you immediately close this window just let me explain. Yes, the name sounds like the result of a "give me a cheesy Christmas rom-com title" ChatGPT prompt, but Randolph alone should pique your interest. The actor has quietly been delivering standout performances in Taylor Sheridan's "Landman" and his "Yellowstone" prequel "1923." The former sees her play Ainsley Norris, the ditzy but determined daughter of Billy Bob Thornton's oil man Tommy Norris. Based on her performances in those demonstrates, Randolph surely has a bright future ahead. While "Clashing Through the Snow" might not be her major breakthrough, it's doing pretty darn well on Prime Video.

Until recently, Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale's sports movie "Madden" was topping the Prime Video charts. But it's now been knocked out of the top spot by this festive romance movie, in which publishing editor Hannah Hendricks (Randolph) is forced to take a road trip with her rival, Ryan Mitchell (Chris Briney). You can see where this is going.

According to streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, the film has now hit number two on the United States overall Prime Video chart (which combines TV and films) as of Thanksgiving day, and sits at number one on the movie chart. But Michelle Randolph's comedy is proving popular elsewhere, too. In fact, it's become a global hit. At the time of writing, the film is charting on 61 countries' top 10 movie rankings, which is a pretty good showing. Even more impressive, "Clashing Through the Snow" is number one on the movie charts in 47 of those countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Meanwhile, the movie has managed to break into the overall chart in 30 countries, taking the top spot in five of them. That means "Clashing Through the Snow" is the most-watched piece of media on Prime Video in Austria, Poland, Portugal, South Africa, and Switzerland. It even managed to hit number one on the overall chart in the U.S. on November 25, 2026. That's a notable achievement, as often films will break into the top 10 movies without making it onto the overall charts. "Clashing Through the Snow" must be good, then...

"Clashing Through the Snow" is a comfortingly familiar rom-com outing that's perfect for the holidays. The film sees Chris Briney's Ryan Mitchell and Michelle Randolph's Hannah Hendricks stranded at an airport during a snowstorm, after which they share a rental car and set out on a cross-country trip to New York. The pair both need to close a deal in order to save their jobs — but wouldn't you know it, they fall in love instead. Along the way there's plenty of romantic Christmas movie moments as the couple stop in charming small towns and overcome mishaps together. Is "Clashing Through the Snow" pushing the boundaries of rom-coms? No. Is it charming? Sure is.

The film is directed by Carlson Young, who made her feature directorial debut with the 2021 fantasy horror "The Blazing World" before directing Sophie Turner in 2025's "Trust." She also oversaw a couple of Prime Video rom-coms before "Clashing Through the Snow," directing 2024's "Upgraded" and 2026's "The Last Sunrise.".

According to recent reports, now, she's delivered a major hit with her Randolph-led Christmas rom-com, which has a 77% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. There aren't enough reviews to earn it a critic score yet, but while William Bibbiani of TheWrap found it to be "unapologetically clichéd" he also found the dialogue to be memorable and saw the film as "an efficient delivery mechanism for semi-believable rom and semi-funny com.".

If that sounds appealing, "Clashing Through the Snow" is streaming on Prime Video right now.

Recent findings suggest that it’s not every day you see a movie where talking sheep get to be the stars. But Kyle Balda’s “The Sheep Detectives” does exactly that. The Amazon MGM film flips the whodunnit formula on its head with a barnyard murder mystery in which a group of sheep have to solve the murder of their beloved shepherd. Much of the film’s success can be attributed to the juxtaposition between a whimsical plot and the realism with which it’s executed. The sheep might talk and solve crimes, but they look like real animals you’d find on any farm.

During the VFX section of IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “The Sheep Detectives” Visual Effects Supervisor Graham Page broke down the meticulous research process that made the sheep look so lifelike. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

According to recent reports, “To make them look real, talking about practical and how key that is, I from Day One felt like you had to base these characters on real sheep,” Page remarked. “We filmed [real sheep] with multiple cameras and getting on boxes. We had a script, almost, like ‘These are the things the sheep need to do in the film.’ Even before an animator can touch it, another artist modeled the skeleton and the muscle and fat. And then you have a rigger and a facial artist, all of these artists.”.

He went on to explain how that research process produced character-defining details that they would not have discovered any other way.

“We started to come up with what we would call ‘Sheep-isms’ that help kind of bring some of that natural movement,” he stated. “There’s a little ear twitch. And a human can’t twitch their ear, but it felt so right. We were like ‘This is really nice,’ and it emphasized the character and the story and the emotion. But it was brought out of a sheep.”.

Bringing one of literature's greatest works to life is no easy task, but Netflix is rising to the challenge with Pride and Prejudice. Written by Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice was her third novel and the second to be published, released in 1813. At the center is the dynamic between Elizabeth Bennet (whose personal growth drives the story) and the proud, wealthy Mr. Darcy. Through their time together, Elizabeth recognizes the mistakes of judging people too swiftly and learns how to distinguish fake charm from true kindness.

Industry observers note that in the century since Pride and Prejudice was published, it has been adapted for the screen several times, beginning with a 1938 BBC television broadcast written and directed by Michael Barry. Unfortunately, that version is permanently lost because it aired live before television recording technology existed. Memorable adaptations include the Academy Award-winning movie starring Greer Garson and Laurence Olivier, partly based on Helen Jerome's 1935 stage adaptation; Joe Wright's acclaimed 2005 feature starring Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen; andthe 1995 BBC miniseries starring Colin Firth and Jennifer Ehle. Now, the upcoming Netflix version joins the bunch, premiering in just one week.

Starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden as Elizabeth and Darcy, Netflix's Pride and Prejudice series was first reported to be in development in October 2024 and officially unveiled in April 2025. Filming began in the UK in the summer of 2025, with first-look behind-the-scenes images released in July. Bestselling author and screenwriter Dolly Alderton wrote the series, and Euros Lyn directed. The six-part series premieres on December 3, 2026, as Alderton announced at the Jane Austen Festival in September.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

In a recent development, you do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Elizabeth, the second of five daughters, faces pressure to marry well or risk losing the comfortable life she knows. As she steps into society, she meets the prickly Mr. Darcy, and their love story unfolds alongside that of her older sister Jane, who falls for the charming Mr. Bingley.

Other stars in the Regency romance adaptation include Olivia Colman as the Bennet family matriarch, Mrs. Bennet; Rufus Sewell as her husband, Mr. Bennet; Freya Mavor as the eldest Bennet daughter, Jane; and Rhea Norwood as Lydia Bennet. Newcomers Hollie Avery and Hopey Parish make their debut roles as Kitty and Mary Bennet, respectively. Daryl McCormack will portray Jane's love interest, Mr. Bingley, while Siena Kelly will play his sister, Caroline Bingley.

Netflix's Pride and Prejudice premieres in one week.

It is an unorthodox sequence. In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs. capitalism for her latest friend Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira). The scene lasts 11 minutes and digs into material you would expect in a university seminar, not the latest cinematic achievement from the Oscar-winning director of “Drive My Car,” Ryūsuke Hamaguchi.

While a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

According to recent reports, and yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes. Now, its distributor, Neon, heads into this weekend’s holiday theatrical release believing it has a legit shot at winning over the more commercially oriented Oscar voters — and becoming one of the (increasingly common) foreign-language Best Picture nominations. Neon similarly released “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” to Best Picture nominations the year before.

The whiteboard scene is not an extraneous aside, but a critical turning point in the women’s relationship. We asked the film’s writer/director why it not only works, but was deemed vital to the film.

“In trying to answer why this somehow works, I think there’s a few layers to it,” remarked Hamaguchi while on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “And one maybe is because it really is something that is far removed from what is generally considered as cinematic. Perhaps because of that, it brings about a certain suspense, where you wonder, ‘OK, what is this for? What is this actually going to do?’ And there’s a certain sense of wondering that happens.”.

Sources indicate that the scene comes a little over an hour into the film. Neither woman wants their magical evening to end. Mari follows Marie-Lou to her job as director of a nursing home, where she struggles to implement her passion project, “Huminitude,” a patient-centered care method based on touch and eye contact, which Mari sees in action. What prompts Mari’s whiteboard seminar is an attempt to help her newly introduced companion put into perspective the resistance she faces in implementing Huminitude and open the door to problem-solving.

According to recent reports, “I think the second part [of why the scene works] really comes down to the efforts of the actors that are performing this scene,” noted Hamaguchi of Okamoto and Efira, who shared the Best Actress Prize at Cannes. “For Tao, I think it was an incredibly difficult scene to perform because first of all she really needed to understand all of the concepts that she was describing here and to really understand everything intellectually. And so in her preparation she did read a lot of the relevant books to really understand what she is talking about.”.

Hamaguchi believes the key to his dialogue-driven film is not necessarily how the words are spoken, but the performance of the listening and how the words are received. In Efira’s whiteboard scene, we see a shift from determined frustration to open enthusiasm that changes the direction of the film itself.

In a recent development, “The attitude of listening that Virginie portrays in this moment, I think, is very vital and really supports this scene,” stated Hamaguchi. “She’s not uninterested in what is going on, but in fact she feels that this is something that she should really be exploring together and she’s there and very much present. And I think this attitude of interest and curiosity really starts to work on the audience as well. And so in that sense I think ultimately this scene really works because of the actors’ performances.”.

One topic that comes up in most post-screening Q&As is that both actresses were not working in the native language. Hamaguchi himself had to work with an interpreter to direct his leads. This is not the first time Hamaguchi has worked this way. On the podcast, he said that, in his experience directing the play inside “Drive My Car,” the language barrier was less of a hindrance and could even aid actors in listening to one another, as shown in the whiteboard scene.

Sources indicate that “I felt that, in fact, this kind of difficulty that exists can in fact provide an environment for even more heightened concentration than you might have if you were speaking the same language,” said Hamaguchi. “ I think that actually when you can actually hear a lot and get a lot of information from somebody’s voice, you can, in fact, precisely feel just how concentrated the person is when they’re saying something by listening to their voice.”.

Asked if any of his collaborators or producers ever questioned the whiteboard scene after reading the script, Hamaguchi said no, and speculated why: “Because it’s so unusual, I think people understood that this is something that I really wanted to do.”.

“There were some questions around, ‘This section feels a little long. Is there anything we can do about that?’” recalled Hamaguchi, adding that he made a concerted effort to cut his four-hour script to a three-hour, 16-minute running time.

“For me, I was ultimately trying to bring in the shortest version that I felt was accurate for this moment. But ultimately, there is this understanding that this moment is a very key turning point within the film, and so I believe that the producers also understood this.”.

“All of a Sudden” is now playing in select theaters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The Hawk,” a Will Ferrell golf comedy that debuted just this summer, has been canceled by Netflix and will not return for a second season, an individual with knowledge told IndieWire.

It has been revealed that ferrell co-created the series in which he plays a former top golfer who is now trying to return to the tour. And while it figured to be a tentpole series for Netflix, one that carried possibly the most expensive budget for a comedy series on Netflix and reunited Ferrell with his “SNL” co-star Molly Shannon and co-creator Harper Steele, it didn’t connect with critics or audiences.

“The Hawk” spent just three weeks on Netflix’s Top 10 when it debuted back in July, topping out at #2 in its second week on Netflix with just 6.2 million views. Ferrell’s vulgar, loudly-dressed golfer with a personalized visor and big mess of bleached blonde hair played a lot like some of Ferrell’s other string of sports comedies throughout the years. But even our critic was perplexed by the series’ tone that makes it sometimes play like a “bizarre addiction drama.” Related Stories ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down.

Steele, in a recent appearance on “Late Night with Seth Meyers,” tipped her hand a little that the show was likely ending when she let slip that, “I was working on a short-lived but probably the best show ever, ‘The Hawk.’”.

The cancellation comes in the wake of a changing of the guard at Netflix, with Peter Rice taking over for veteran creative chief Bela Bajaria. Our critic also recently wrote about the challenges Netflix is facing right now in getting audiences to discover new series in the ways they used to.

But at the same time, Netflix has already renewed a couple of other comedy series that even premiered after “The Hawk” later this year, including “Nobody Wants This,” “A Different World,” “Tires,” “Massive Mistakes,” and “The Four Seasons.” Netflix is also still working with Ferrell’s Gloria Sanchez Productions on three new series, “All the Rage,” “Prep,” and another scripted series from Nikki Glaser.

Deadline first reported the news.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that magneto's biggest costume redesign is coming to the X-Men's upcoming reboot, with an older Master of Magnetism donning the suit to fight entire armies. All Magneto truly needs to be instantly recognized anywhere in pop culture is his signature helmet and a flowing cape. Functionally, the horn-rimmed helmet shields Max Eisenhardt’s mind from Charles Xavier’s telepathy, but visually, it crowns him like a defiant warrior-king who refuses to bow to human authority. Magneto's cape billows dramatically whenever he hovers through the air on magnetic fields, signaling his status as mutantkind’s self-appointed sovereign and protector.

Marvel artists have reinvented Magneto’s wardrobe for more than six decades of X-Men comics. His classic 1963 crimson-and-violet uniform established his bold appearance before later eras introduced fresh designs. Magneto wore his sleeveless purple-and-magenta trial jumpsuit during Chris Claremont’s Uncanny X-Men #200, and his battle-worn armor with flowing silver hair in Age of Apocalypse. Later on, Cullen Bunn’s Uncanny X-Men run introduced an armored black-and-red revolutionary suit, and the Ultimate Universe put an elegant spin on Magneto's classic costume with a simple combination of a red suit, a black cape, and a black helmet.

Magneto's costumes tend to be so beautifully designed that one arc or series is never enough to do them justice.

Recent findings suggest that R.B. Silva's Midnight X-Men concept art previously revealed a more traditional-looking costume design for the Midnight Universe's Magneto, sporting a dark purple helmet and an elegant coat covering a sharp combo of dark vest and dark pants. However, Declan Shalvey's variant cover for Midnight X-Men #4 reveals a very different costume. Magneto is depicted using his powers to annihilate an entire vampire army, his sleeveless white Marvel NOW! suit shining bright, with a large white cape flowing in the wind as he descends from the sky with his arms spread out.

In a universe where mutants and humans wage a war for survival against a vampire horde, Midnight X-Men's Magneto acts as a cleansing force against the undead plague, flanked by fellow mutants like Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver. Magneto's decision to wear a gleaming white suit instead of his classic crimson-and-violet war colors reinforces his purifying mission in this timeline. Although he tends to abandon his extremist methods gradually with every shared threat he faces alongside the X-Men all across the Marvel multiverse, Midnight X-Men's version of Magneto has moved past conquering humanity to become mutantkind's shining shield quite prematurely.

Industry observers note that after seven live-action movies from X-Men to Dark Phoenix, both Ian McKellen and Michael Fassbender wore several variations of Magneto’s classic red-and-purple armor or dark trench coats, never once suiting up in anything resembling the striking white-and-chrome ensemble made famous in Jonathan Hickman’s late-2010s House of X. Besides translating the gleaming white suit to the significant screen for the very first time, and besides honoring one of Magneto's most celebrated comic-book designs of the modern era, Marvel could signal a fresh era for Magneto's stories on the big screen where none of his previous movie arcs are repeated.

Fox's X-Men movies spent several installments and multiple timeline resets on Erik Lehnsherr’s slow transformation into a mutant extremist and back into a reluctant anti-hero, and Avengers: Doomsday adds Ian McKellen's Magneto to the X-Men's lineup as a seasoned and fully heroic member. The MCU's X-Men reboot can skip repetitive villain origin beats and align Magneto with Charles Xavier and the X-Men far sooner and symbolize his genuine intentions to be a hero with an all-white costume that mirrors his Krakoan heroism. In fact, considering Marvel Studios may explore everything Fox didn't cover, Magneto's white costume could easily debut in a direct Krakoan-era movie.

What's your favorite Magneto look?

7 Sci-Fi Books That Are Better Than 'Neuromancer'

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1239 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cyberpunk wouldn't be what it is today without Neuromancer.
  • However, Neuromancer can be a difficult and disorienting read for some.
  • Set in a dystopian 21st century, Snow Crash depicts a Los Angeles that is vividly different, one where corporations rule and governments falter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cyberpunk wouldn't be what it is today without Neuromancer. Long before computers and the Internet became part of everyday life, sci-fi writers were already imagining what the world might look like with such technology, but more importantly, how it would affect humanity. Neuromancer is one of those books, imagining a dystopian society controlled by global computer networks and introducing hackers like Case, who push the boundaries of artificial intelligence.

However, Neuromancer can be a difficult and disorienting read for some. While it's an essential part of the genre, other books explore similar ideas in ways that some readers might find more engaging. From a cyberpunk reimagining of an American classic to stories about mind-controlling viruses, here are sci-fi books that are better than Neuromancer.

Set in a dystopian 21st century, Snow Crash depicts a Los Angeles that is vividly different, one where corporations rule and governments falter. By day, Hiro Protagonist is a Mafia pizza delivery driver. By night, he's a freelance hacker. When a mysterious digital drug called Snow Crash causes a fellow hacker to suffer brain damage, Hiro gets to the bottom of it—only to discover a sinister conspiracy that could endanger not only the lives of Angelians, but the entire world.

Recent findings suggest that casual sci-fi fans who find Neuromancer a tough read may prefer Snow Crash. Neal Stephenson's novel is more accessible and entertaining than Gibson's noir-inspired classic, but still offers plenty of investigative intrigue. Its cyberspace is also easier to picture, with virtual worlds, customizable avatars, and interconnected networks that feel familiar today. Published over three decades ago, Snow Crash remains relevant, especially in its depiction of a world where corporations control entire territories.

Industry observers note that forget F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby—K.M. Fajardo gives the American classic a cyberspace twist in Local Heavens. The year is 2075, and Filipino-American Nick Carraway has moved to Fresh York City, now dubbed the Fractured New Americas. Towering skyscrapers loom over the city, while the slums of the working middle class lie beneath them. But despite cynicism over capitalism, Nick can't help but be charmed by the charismatic new-money Jay Gatsby.

Bringing hacking into a familiar tale of admiration, love, and jealousy might seem like an odd choice, but Local Heavens makes it work by giving Nick's mission a personal angle. Unlike Neuromancer, where hacking serves a larger heist, it becomes a source of emotional conflict here. Nick is a corporate-sanctioned hacker assigned to investigate Jay, but the deeper he gets into Jay's world of wealthy people using technology to cheat death, the more he finds himself drawn to Jay, putting his mission at risk.

In The Shockwave Rider, America has become a dystopia where government agencies and corporations have near-total control over computer networks. Not everyone is willing to play along, especially Nick Haflinger, a gifted programmer on the run from Tarnover, a secret program that trained him to serve the state. Armed with a stolen access code, he manipulates the network to stay one step ahead of his pursuers. But one wrong move could expose him and put him right back in their hands.

For a novel published more than half a century ago, it's mind-blowing how prophetic The Shockwave Rider is, especially since the internet was still in its infancy. While Neuromancer imagines cyberspace as a high-concept medium accessible only through neural interfaces, The Shockwave Rider demonstrates how cyberspace is much closer to our personal lives, with computer networks connecting homes, offices, and public terminals. It also offers a sharper look at surveillance culture, showing how easily institutions can access and exploit our personal data.

According to recent reports, if you've watched the Blade Runner movies, it's imperative that you read the original novel it's based on. Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? is set on a post-apocalyptic Earth where radioactive fallout has driven most animals to extinction. Rick Deckard, a San Francisco bounty hunter, hopes to earn enough money to replace his electric sheep by hunting six rogue androids that have escaped from Mars.

Sources indicate that people often talk about artificial intelligence as if artificial beings are nothing more than machines. While that may be true in a technical sense, Dick challenges this assumption by exploring the philosophical implications of AI rather than just its mechanics. He questions whether artificial beings deserve the same empathy, freedom, and dignity as humans, especially when supposedly empathetic people demonstrate cruelty and indifference toward other living beings. As AI becomes increasingly humanlike, Dick's questions about what separates humans from machines feel more relevant than ever.

According to recent reports, nobody is safe in Gnomon. In an alternate, futuristic Britain, an all-seeing AI keeps the population under constant surveillance. Government investigator Mielikki Neith is assigned to investigate the death of Diana Hunter, who died during a forced extraction of her memories. But as Neith examines Hunter's recorded thoughts, she uncovers something far more disturbing than a suspicious death: a hidden danger that could expose the surveillance system's nature and threaten the society built around it.

It has been revealed that gnomon may not share Neuromancer's cyberspace premise, but it offers a different, equally unsettling vision of technological control. When technology becomes the infrastructure of an entire society, surveillance extends beyond tracking people's physical movements to probing their thoughts and memories. Nick Harkaway's novel raises urgent questions about privacy and consent for ordinary people, concerns that feel especially timely in an internet age when personal data is constantly collected, stored, and exposed without people's knowledge or permission.

In a technologically advanced future, artificial intelligence has evolved beyond human comprehension in Void Star. Only a select few can interpret its thoughts, making them valuable assets. Told from three perspectives, the novel follows Irina, a corporate consultant who translates AI-generated thoughts; Thales, the son of a Brazilian politician; and Kern, a streetwise thief raised in the favelas. Their lives collide when Irina and Thales discover that someone can remotely extract memories stored in their cranial implants.

Zachary Mason's Void Star is essentially Neuromancer for readers who want cyberpunk that feels closer to the world we live in today. Building on the ideas established by Gibson, the novel brings them into a future shaped by climate change, mass displacement, autonomous weapons, and extreme wealth inequality. Although the story follows three main characters, the shifting perspectives are easy to follow and add nuance by showing how each experiences the same technological and social problems.

It has been revealed that death is no longer an concern in Altered Carbon. Set 350 years in the future, Richard K. Morgan's novel imagines a world where cortical stacks implanted in people's spines store their consciousness, allowing them to transfer into new bodies called sleeves. But immortality doesn’t come cheap. The wealthy can afford replacement bodies and backups, while poorer people still risk dying for good. In this world, staying alive even depends on how much money you have.

While Neuromancer explores cyberspace, corporate AI, and crime through an investigative plot, Altered Carbon brings those technological anxieties into the human body. Its technology can preserve consciousness, but it can't resolve the moral questions that come with it, from bodily ownership to the privilege of living forever. Morgan takes Neuromancer's criticism of capitalism and makes it more personal, turning it into a dilemma about bodily autonomy and how far people are willing to go to preserve their lives.

Industry News: What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone.
  • That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.
  • Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

Recent findings suggest that at the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”.

In a recent development, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

It has been revealed that thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

Recent findings suggest that and in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

In a recent development, there are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

It has been revealed that after years of pure torture in Earth's Hell, trapped in a cocoon surrounded by singing fairies and dancing angels, Frieza is finally back in Dragon Ball Super: Beerus. The enhanced remake spent its first six episodes tightening up the God of Destruction Beerus saga, but episode #7, “Resurrection 'F',” brought the Emperor of the Universe back into the picture. Sorbet and Tagoma used Earth's Dragon Balls to revive him, and now episode #8 is ready to kick the Golden Frieza saga into full gear.

That makes this a big test for Toei Animation. The original Dragon Ball Super TV retelling of Resurrection 'F' became infamous in 2015 for its rushed schedule, something that even the creator, Akira Toriyama, was unhappy about. Frieza's return deserves a lot better, especially after the remake has spent weeks showing just how much the studio can improve the old material.

Taking over One Piece's Sunday slot on Fuji TV, this 19-episode remake has been on a roll since its October premiere. Toei trimmed the original 14-episode Beerus arc down to six tight installments, cutting out dragged-out fights and overblown gags while giving the visuals a major facelift. If episode #8 keeps that same energy going through Frieza's comeback, Dragon Ball Super: Beerus could set the stage perfectly for the upcoming Dragon Ball Super: The Galactic Patrol anime, which will adapt the Moro arc.

In a recent development, dragon Ball Super: Beerus episode #8, titled “Revenge 'F',” officially premieres on Sunday, November 29, 2026, at 8:00 AM PST / 11:00 AM EST (4:00 PM GMT) on Crunchyroll and Hulu. It will also be accessible through Disney+. Meanwhile, Netflix viewers in the US will have to wait a little longer, as episode #8 won’t arrive on the platform until Saturday, December 5, making it a six-day delay.

Australian Eastern Daylight Time (AEDT).

The English dub is also underway on Crunchyroll, with Sean Schemmel and Christopher R. Sabat back as Goku and Vegeta. Dubbed episodes aren’t released simultaneously with the Japanese version, though. Upcoming episodes drop on Thursdays at 8:00 AM PT, and the dub is right now running roughly five episodes behind Japan after launching on November 12.

Now that Frieza has been pieced back together aboard Sorbet’s ship, it’s time for the tyrant to get back to work. Episode #8 moves into his infamous four-month training run, the one that leads to his Golden form. Meanwhile, Goku and Vegeta are training under Whis on Beerus’s planet, working toward Super Saiyan Blue. With Toei Animation keeping this 19-episode remake moving at a much snappier pace, there’s little reason to expect the studio to spend too long getting Frieza and his 1,000-soldier army to Earth.

The episode is also expected to close on a hype note, with Gohan, Piccolo, and the rest of the Z Fighters holding the line while they wait for Goku and Vegeta. That’s a familiar setup, but Resurrection 'F' has a decade of baggage to deal with. The original story drew plenty of criticism for its messy power scaling, and tracksuit Gohan remains one of the saga’s most infamous choices. Cleaner animation is a welcome start, but Toei needs tighter storytelling to make this return land.

According to recent reports, after wrapping up the God of Destruction Beerus saga in just six episodes, Dragon Ball Super: Beerus isn’t slowing down for Frieza’s comeback. With the remake reportedly set for 19 episodes covering the Beerus, Golden Frieza, and Universe 6 sagas, the Resurrection 'F' retelling could be done in just six or seven more. That would leave room for Champa’s tournament, while cutting a lot of fat from the 2015 anime, which spent 13 episodes on Frieza’s return alone and more than 40 on all three arcs.

The story may be familiar from the movie and the original TV anime, but this remake is giving it a fresh shot. Toei’s tighter pacing and reworked visuals are already making a difference. Now episode #8 has to keep that momentum going, because Frieza’s return deserves more than a prettier rerun. If the remake can stick the landing here, Dragon Ball Super: Beerus might finally deliver the sharp opening run this series should have had from the start.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” stated recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”.

Recent findings suggest that though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” said Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.” Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

The coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”.

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the New Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks noted “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”.

She stated, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal challenges and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Industry observers note that having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks noted “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”.

Sources indicate that one job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the New Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” stated Brooks.

Sources indicate that “We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she stated. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”.

It has been revealed that since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”.

“If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they remarked, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

In a recent development, she continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”.

One of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she stated. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”.

Sources indicate that on the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” mentioned Brooks.

It has been revealed that but regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is important,” said the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that big machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”.

According to recent reports, “Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” said Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”.

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.
