The 10 Worst Oscars Decisions of All Time, Ranked

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ah, the Academy Awards.
  • Industry observers note that from brutal robberies to jaw-dropping shocks, when the Oscars botch it, we make our opinions loud and clear.
  • Perhaps this category had many people in shock the moment the nominations were declared because it meant that Eurovision Song Contest: Story of Fire Saga was an Oscar nominee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ah, the Academy Awards. Every year, cinephiles tune in for the massive event as the Oscars honor the best of the best of the previous year in cinema. And like most viewers, opinions are not only present; everybody has one. While those opinions usually arrive the day nominations are officially revealed, they linger well beyond when the sealed envelope is opened, and the winner is revealed. In the almost century the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has handed out the gold statuette, a handful of decisions have left us baffled.

Industry observers note that from brutal robberies to jaw-dropping shocks, when the Oscars botch it, we make our opinions loud and clear. There are certainly more than ten times that they’ve made the wrong decision; these ten are the absolute worst. Perhaps it was the fact that some of the greatest films of all time were beaten out, or the voters were too prejudiced to make a bold decision; these horrible wins meant deserving projects, performers, and creators lost. Though some individuals earned their award at another time, others are still waiting. While the biggest travesty in Academy Awards history is that Glenn Close doesn’t have a performance trophy, these other decisions continue to have us scratching our heads.

Perhaps this category had many people in shock the moment the nominations were declared because it meant that Eurovision Song Contest: Story of Fire Saga was an Oscar nominee. But the truth is, its nomination was well warranted. And it’s not just because I’m a die-hard Eurovision fanatic. Their entry, “Husavik (My Hometown),” is actually a remarkable track. Unfortunately, even with a stunning performance from Molly Sandén “live” on a boat in Iceland with an Icelandic child choir on Oscar night, it was still not enough to sway voters. Instead, the honor was given to “Fight for You” from Judas and the Black Messiah. The song authentically captured the late-1960s soul and funk sound of the film while speaking directly to contemporary themes of racial injustice.

According to recent reports, performed by H.E.R. with music by H.E.R. and Dernst Emile II, with lyrics by H.E.R. and Tiara Thomas, the song addresses racism, police brutality, and state repression, linking Hampton's story and COINTELPRO to modern racial justice movements. Its message aligned closely with broader racial justice conversations and H.E.R.'s recent Grammy Song of the Year win for "I Can't Breathe.” Though a great song, it had momentum to ride on. Though it changed drastically, as we’ll discuss later, the Academy voting trends often favor socially urgent anthems over comedic or parody films. For those familiar with the source material on which Eurovision Song Contest: Story of Fire Saga is based, “Husavik (My Hometown)” likely would have met a victory there. Nevertheless, at least the Will Ferrell comedy got an Oscar nod!

Margaret Thatcher is known for many things. From the infamous “The lady’s not for turning” to earning the nickname “Iron Lady,” she was ripe for a biopic. And if anyone was going to play her, one might think it would be a Brit. But the next best option is Meryl Streep. The legendary actress has a mantel full of Oscars and plenty of nominations to go with them. For her turn as Maggie Thatcher, it should have been simply another nomination as the win should have been given to Viola Davis for The Help. Streep was widely praised for capturing Thatcher's posture, voice, and steely resolve while finding the human vulnerability beneath the political figure. But it was by no means her strongest performance. In fact, a major factor in her victory was the headline: Streep’s third Oscar win ended a 29-year drought after 12 straight defeats.

Industry observers note that while Streep did earn the Golden Globe and BAFTA, a precursor to the Oscar win, the film itself wasn’t well received. Her victory may have stemmed from reverence. It gave voters a long-overdue milestone moment. Distributor Harvey Weinstein ran a heavy awards push for The Iron Lady, and at the time, it carried a lot of weight. Although Davis won the Screen Actors Guild Award and The Help was a box-office hit, the film lacked directing or writing nominations and also had running mate Octavia Spencer competing for acting recognition. Davis finally earned a victory on her third try for Best Supporting Actress for her performance as Rose in Fences.

As will be a trend moving forward, Best Picture wins are quite a touchy topic. One of the most shocking results from the ‘90s was when Shakespeare in Love beat out the war masterpiece Saving Private Ryan. The romantic dramedy reimagines a young, cash-strapped William Shakespeare (Joseph Fiennes) overcoming severe writer's block when he falls passionately in love with Viola de Lesseps (Gwyneth Paltrow), a wealthy noblewoman who disguises herself as a man to audition for his latest play, inspiring him to write Romeo and Juliet. It sounds like a lovely film, but was it the best of the year? Once again, producer Harvey Weinstein and Miramax pushed the film with an aggressive, politically inspired campaign.

Industry observers note that shakespeare in Love led all films with 13 Oscar nominations, ahead of Saving Private Ryan’s 11, and won the Screen Actors Guild ensemble award. As was clear, voters favored the lighter, witty romance over a grueling war drama, while Steven Spielberg still took home Best Director for Saving Private Ryan. Timing was also a potential factor, as Shakespeare in Love opened in December 1998 and expanded into early 1999 right as voting began, whereas Saving Private Ryan came out in July 1998. Campaigners reportedly pushed the narrative that Saving Private Ryan peaked in its opening D-Day sequence and dragged afterward. With Spielberg reportedly refusing to engage in similar mudslinging or aggressive counter-campaigning, Shakespeare in Love benefited from winning a campaign war.

Sources indicate that life is like a box of chocolates. Forrest Gump remains one of the most iconic films of the '90s. It's no coincidence that it beat out an equally iconic '90s classic: Pulp Fiction. But one was a safe film, and the other was a daring cinematic risk. Directed by Robert Zemeckis, Forrest Gump stars Tom Hanks as the kind-hearted, slow-witted Alabama man as he recounts his extraordinary life while unknowingly influencing major moments in 20th-century American history and pining for his lifelong love, Jenny Curran (Robin Wright). Forrest Gump was a film that was rooted in nostalgia. And for that, it received extra love. With broad emotional appeal and a less polarizing concept, Forrest Gump stood in great contrast to Pulp Fiction, which featured graphic violence and non-traditional morality that clashed with the mainstream Oscar taste of the time.

Forrest Gump was a massive commercial hit with star power and established pedigree. Coming off his win for Philadelphia, Forrest Gump was a crowd-pleaser. It also, for the time, stood out for its technical innovation in which its invisible CGI seamlessly inserted the performers into archival footage, helping it sweep six Oscars overall. And if it won the minor awards, of course the significant one was it as well. The clash between the two films highlighted a great divide between traditional sentimentality and '90s postmodernism. Pulp Fiction's risky storytelling was awarded as Quentin Tarantino won for Best Original Screenplay, but the gritty, non-linear crime story was ahead of its time. Tarantino has argued that the Golden Globes placing the film in the drama category over Musical or Comedy hurt its chances, as it established a specific serious tone for award season despite its dark humor. Nevertheless, when we examine the best films of the decade, Pulp Fiction and even the other big loser, The Shawshank Redemption, tend to be placed above Forrest Gump.

Recent findings suggest that academy voters have great reverence for industry legends, especially when they've built a steadfast career without a win. So, while Jamie Lee Curtis was arguably in the greatest film of the year, was she actually the best supporting actress in that film? Everything Everywhere All at Once remains one of the most triumphant stories of the 2020s. The daring multi-genre film defied the odds, rightly earning all of the praise it received. At the Oscars, it won seven of the 11 nominations it was up for, but the controversial win was when it beat itself. Curtis won for Best Supporting Actress playing IRS inspector Deidre Beaubeidre, blending comedy, action, and emotional weight, even when she sported a bob and hot dog hands. She defeated her co-star, Stephanie Hsu, and it likely came down to a mix of career-long goodwill, strategic campaigning, and late-season awards momentum.

Industry observers note that as an industry veteran, Curtis' win was a career win for her memorable, vanity-free performance. She was a scene-stealer in a character role compared to Hsu's double parts as Joy Wang and Jobu Tupaki. To some, Tsu was the emotional core and a co-lead. And, unfortunately, she would had no shot against Michelle Yeoh should she have been placed in that category. While Hsu has downplayed and dismissed any rivalry, sharing support and happiness for Curtis' win, many people believed that Hsu's loss undercut the importance of spotlighting Asian visibility that came with the film. Perhaps it came down to some unfortunate vote-splitting, or it was all about Curtis' grassroots championing of the film and her impactful off-the-cuff SAG Award acceptance speech, but Hsu was snubbed for an equally incredible performance.

Recent findings suggest that for many of these entries, we're focusing on a one-on-one race. Except for this one. The King's Speech defeated so many incredible films that we're all still baffled. Let's discuss. In the Tom Hooper film, the story follows Britain's reluctant King George VI (Colin Firth) as he works with an unorthodox Australian speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), to overcome a debilitating stammer before addressing his nation at the start of World War II. Biopics tend to do well at the Oscars. It was no different here. Yet it faced heavy hitters, including Black Swan, Inception, The Social Network, and True Grit. So, how was it victorious? The King's Speech combined broad crowd-pleasing appeal, acclaimed acting performances, typical Oscar-bait storytelling, and preferential treatment.

Many have pointed to The King's Speech's classic prestige as a natural fit for traditional voters. Especially during a ranked-choice voting system, which tends to reward films with broader backing rather than divisive favorites. Yet history has shown that its competitors are the films that truly stood the test of time. As an inspiring, emotionally accessible choice with strong above-the-line wins, it was not enough for the other films to overcome the hurdle. The Social Network emerged as its biggest competitor, having a strong early push, but lost out in crucial categories. Inception rightly achieved four technical Oscars, but its voters were not on board for the high-concept sci-fi thriller. Natalie Portman won for Black Swan, but when Clint Mansell's score was disqualified from Oscar consideration for relying heavily on Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake, the film lost most of its momentum. And True Grit went 0-for-10. Needless to say, the 83rd Academy Awards was a doozy!

It's time to journey back to 1941 when one of the greatest films ever made, Citizen Kane, won the Academy Award for Best Picture. Scratch that. When it LOST the Academy Award for Best Picture. Mind-blowing! One of the biggest shockers in Oscar history came down to a preference for nostalgia, a beloved director, and a media mogul's fervent push to prevent a victory. Citizen Kane failed to win Best Picture, losing to How Green Was My Valley. Based on the book by Richard Llewellyn, the John Ford drama follows youngest son Huw Morgan (Roddy McDowall) as he looks back on his close-knit family's joys, labor struggles, and gradual dissolution in a turn-of-the-century South Wales coal-mining town. How Green Was My Valley was victorious for its combined prestige, studio craftsmanship, and emotional family drama with wartime appeal. Having come off of back-to-back Best Director wins, Ford set the industry standard. Orson Welles made a mark in a very different way.

Recent findings suggest that 25-year-old Welles, a relative newcomer to the industry, faced the ire of newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst, making voters wary of backing it. Hearst viewed Citizen Kane as a personal attack and used his newspapers to suppress coverage and hurt the film's box office. Welles was seen as a brash outsider disrupting studio norms, using themes of power and isolation to tell his story. His confidence ruffled feathers, resulting in the film's punishment. That stated, Citizen Kane wasn't viewed as the masterpiece we see it as today. Following Pearl Harbor, How Green Was My Valley was the safer, more comforting option. This defeat remains one of the more peculiar decisions in Oscar history.

The 2003 Academy Awards were quite controversial. The ceremony was well before cancel culture was the way of the world, so artistic merit outweighed personal conflict. So Roman Polanski's Best Director win for The Pianist wasn't because he didn't deserve it for his work, but the shock came from his troubled past. After widespread critical acclaim, Polanski earned the award through his deep personal connection to the material. Polanski survived the Holocaust as a child, which mirrored the survival themes within the source material. Between his passion behind the project and the belief that he had "paid his dues," Academy voters gave him the win. But he did not attend the ceremony because he remained a fugitive from the U.S. justice system since he pleaded guilty in 1978, ahead of sentencing, to unlawful sexual intercourse with a minor. His victory drew cheers and a standing ovation from parts of the audience, but it sparked a debate over separating an artist's personal crimes from their creative work.

According to recent reports, had voters opted to give the win to another director, the options were Martin Scorsese for Gangs of New York and Rob Marshall for Chicago. It should be noted that the latter won for Best Picture. A major reason these two frontrunners lost was vote splitting. Scorsese won the Golden Globe while Marshall won the DGA Award. This opened the door for Polanski's upset. Despite Chicago's win, some long-time voters were not thrilled at the notion of honoring Marshall for his feature film debut. Gangs of New York also faced campaign backlash over Miramax's promotional tactics. While the overdue sentiment was overwhelmingly felt, Polanski's victory will forever be marred by controversy.

Recent findings suggest that surely you remember Art Carney's beloved performance as Harry Coombes in Harry and Tonto! Surely it's up to the same standard as Al Pacino as Michael Corleone in The Godfather Part II and Jack Nicholson as J.J. "Jake" Gittes in Chinatown! Yeah, that's a bald-faced lie! And yet, it was Carney who won the Academy Award for Best Actor. Carney was recognized for his warm, understated performance as an evicted elderly widower traveling across America with his cat. Playing a 70-something at 55 with heavy makeup, Carney delivered a low-key, relatable portrayal full of heart and dignity. Yet extreme vote splitting between the Hollywood heavyweights kept the admired contenders off the Oscar stage. It should be noted that they also had to compete against Albert Finney in Murder on the Orient Express and Dustin Hoffman for Lenny, so needless to say, it was a tough year to be any of those men!

Against darker, more intense roles, Carney emerged as the safe, feel-good alternative. It was a win for a TV veteran who made a rare major big-screen leading turn. But there may be more to the story. At least for Pacino. Some believe his earlier boycott of the 1972 ceremony and The Godfather Part II's major award sweep gave voters the leeway to deny him a trophy. The Godfather dynasty may have worked against Pacino, but why did Nicholson not emerge victorious? It may have come down to Chinatown's bleak, cynical ending, which went against Hollywood standards at the time. Though he may not have won for Chinatown, he did win a year later for One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.

Recent findings suggest that not going to lie, this one still stings. Surely Jack Nicholson read the wrong name, like the whole Moonlight-La La Land kerfuffle, right? Unfortunately, that was not the case, as Crash was victorious at the 2004 ceremony. Directed by Paul Haggis, Crash follows the interconnected lives of several strangers from diverse racial, cultural, and social backgrounds in post 9/11 Los Angeles whose paths unexpectedly collide over a volatile 36-hour period, forcing them to confront prejudice, bigotry, and urban disconnect. The film won thanks to strong support from its massive ensemble, an aggressive DVD screener campaign, and cultural pushback against its rival, Brokeback Mountain. Yes, you read that right. The gay cowboy film was too progressive for the time.

Industry observers note that lionsgate sent over 100,0000 screeners to SAG members and other voters. Because actors formed the largest branch of the Academy, Crash was at the forefront of voters' minds. After winning the SAG Award for Best Ensemble, the momentum shifted toward the film in the stretch toward the Oscars. Oprah Winfrey featured the ensemble on her show. Roger Ebert championed the film as the top movie of the year. But Academy Award voters had to reckon with the fact that Ang Lee's brilliant film may have caused some discomfort. Brokeback Mountain was groundbreaking not just for highlighting a gay romance, but also for being set against a lush Western backdrop and disregarding the genre's tropes. There's no denying Crash's cultural impact, as it was essentially a Haggis passion project, but Brokeback Mountain pushed boundaries by celebrating a same-sex romance and focusing on the hardships of a taboo relationship through the lens of identity. Brokeback Mountain didn't leave the ceremony empty-handed, winning three Oscars for Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay, and Best Original Score, but the supposed anti-gay bias and its subversion of classic Western masculinity became a voter turn-off.

In a recent development, for adventurers and outdoor enthusiasts who want more than the average smartwatch, Garmin sets the standard with its industry-leading features and durability. But while the brand is on many wishlists, its high price tags stop many shoppers from making the splurge. Fortunately, with Amazon’s early Black Friday sale, you can get one of its bestsellers, the 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED, for 44% off at $249.99 (originally $449.99).

The 1.2-inch color AMOLED display makes the screen more readable in bright daylight conditions, and battery life is best-in-class, lasting up to 18 days (even longer when you’re not using it regularly), which reduces the need for weekly charging, a must for those going off-grid. Durability is also a major perk, with features like a metal-reinforced bezel, chemically strengthened glass, and a 10 ATM water rating, which makes it suitable for underwater activities.

It comes with a built-in flashlight and multi-band GPS, supported by Garmin’s SatIQ technology to better balance location accuracy and battery use, while tracking features include heart rate, sleep, blood oxygen, and other wellness metrics. There’s no shortage of training tools for workouts and outdoor activities, and like regular smartwatches, it displays alerts like texts and emails when paired with an iPhone or Android. The Garmin Pay feature is another bonus for those who don’t want to have their wallet on them at all times.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to log your activities, whether that’s skiing the slopes, heading out on a long trail run, or going on a camping trip in the woods, the 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED is a rugged option with plenty of useful tools for those who love the outdoors. And you can’t forget its wildly impressive battery life. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vanessa Piña has been writing as a journalist for over two years. As a senior writer, she focuses on timely coverage of the latest anime releases and popular comic franchises.

Worldbuilding is an essential part of any fantasy series, as a well-defined setting helps viewers understand a society's magical elements, supernatural creatures, and physical laws, allowing them to become immersed in the story. Striking the right balance is, in itself, a difficult task, since although some entries in the genre offer a detailed exposition of their settings, few series manage to integrate their fantastical elements in an original way. However, one underrated Netflix series has one of streaming's most unconventional and twisted magic worlds.

Recent findings suggest that dorohedoro is what happens when the darker elements of fantasy storytelling are pushed to a whole newly introduced level, resulting in an extremely quirky and fascinating journey. Rated TV-MA on Netflix, which makes sense, given how explosively violent it is, Dorohedoro doesn’t use disturbing imagery merely for shock value; instead, its gore serves to illustrate the social structure and the internal logic of its universe.

It has been revealed that released in 2020 by MAPPA, the studio behind hit series such as Jujutsu Kaisen and Attack on Titan, Dorohedoro features one of the most distinctive worlds in anime, characterized by an industrial aesthetic and a chaotic society that can only be brought to the screen through animation. The series is based on the seinen manga by Q Hayashida, which is aimed at adult readers and widely considered a masterpiece within this demographic, making it an essential work for any fan of dark fantasy.

In a recent development, scrolling through Netflix's catalog, it is easy to find fantasy series that focus on hard worldbuilding, which prioritizes establishing complex rules to explain their magical elements. In this regard, Dorohedoro is one of the few series that successfully employs soft worldbuilding by avoiding exhausting lore dumps and over-explaining its mechanics, instead throwing viewers in a disordered dystopian setting that aligns with the story's tone.

The series follows Caiman, a man whose head has been magically transformed into that of a lizard and lost his memory. Armed only with a human head, which mysteriously sits inside his mouth and serves as a means of identification, and accompanied by his friend Nikaido, Caiman is set to find the sorcerer who cursed him, seeking both revenge and the truth about his identity. That way, Dorohedoro creates a unique atmosphere where viewers are just as confused as Caiman, using each bit of information provided to gradually piece together how the world and the magic of the sorcerers function.

That stated, what makes Dorohedoro truly brilliant is the stark contrast between its two settings: the Sorcerers' World and The Hole, the latter being the desolate place where Caiman and Nikaido reside and where sorcerers ruthlessly harm its inhabitants to practice magic. The result is a world that feels alive in every respect, from the dynamics between those who live in The Hole and the sorcerers to the characters' side jobs outside acting as sorcerer hunters and the creative ways the series illustrates the consequences of using magic, as seen in the annual event "The Night of the Living Dead.".

It has been revealed that beyond its world-building and the intriguing mystery surrounding Caiman’s true identity, the charm of Dorohedoro is that it's a rather touching series. Even with its body horror, brutal killings, and abundance of gore, the anime is heartwarming at its core, incorporating dark comedy and lighthearted moments of camaraderie, showing the small joys in life such as sharing a meal. This makes the 23 episodes of Dorohedoro, spread across two seasons, particularly easy to binge-watch.

Sources indicate that the best part is that Dorohedoro still has plenty of story left to tell. With the anime having adapted around 80 chapters, it has reached roughly the halfway point of the manga. Fortunately, Dorohedoro Season 3 has already been confirmed.

The board of directors, however, said that it had no intention of inviting him back.

Nvidia’s chair Harvey Jones remarked: “The board does not intend to reinstate him.”.

That changed today, with the firm making the announcement in a press release.

Nvidia today declared that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

Sources indicate that “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a newly introduced industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”.

Recent findings suggest that as previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. Recent findings suggest that amid all the sex and murder in “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 — and there is a lot of sex and murder — the riskiest scene suspends itself between the two. Sophie (Brittany Snow), an East Coast liberal out of place in the conservative Texas town of Maple Brook, and Margo (Malin Åkerman), the mysterious local matriarch who can wrap just about anyone around her finely manicured fingertips, are confronted with a fresh dilemma. For spoilers sake, I won’t get into specifics, but the concern is urgent and impacts them both, without being serious enough to warrant what turns out to be their first-thought fix:.

In a recent development, in the moment, their lethal instinct seems reasonable. Margo already shot a pregnant teenager in the woods, and Sophie committed vehicular homicide against Margo’s brother (which invited suspicions about Sophie’s past, considering its eerie similarities to a deadly “accident” back in Massachusetts). Their friends, neighbors, and even a youth pastor met their maker, too — just in the first season! So what’s one more body to bury? Go on! Kill ’em! Get yours! Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season.

But before their bloodlust gets the best of them, their better angels make one last plea. Margo hesitates. Sophie follows suit. The gears start turning as they stare into each other’s wide, worried eyes: Are they really prepared to take another life? Are people that disposable to them? What does their initial response say about how they’ve changed? What does it mean about who they’ve become?

No need to spoil what happens next. The pause makes all the difference. “The Hunting Wives” has always been self-aware, but Margo and Sophie’s recognition of slaughter as their default response to trouble is a critical moment in a second season that reloads without slowing down. Creator Rebecca Cutler knows her Netflix soap is careening past the point where its central couple can reasonably return to lives lived between Margarita Mondays and Sunday church. Killing again, so quickly and carelessly, puts them on the precipice of becoming Bonnie and Clyde Bonnie — known fugitives who are only out for each other. Taking a beat lends the series a critical perspective — a vantage point from the top of the roller coaster, right before the substantial drop, where you can appreciate for a few brief, fleeting seconds the insanity to come.

Then you’re flying. You (and Margo and Sophie) are convinced it’s better to just move forward. Heck, this crisis isn’t going to fix itself!

Margo and Sophie’s breakneck pace to break necks is mostly a feature in Netflix’s surprise hit. The high-key camp comedy and low-key conservative satire moves quickly, sure, but where its characters are often flustered and panicked, it’s decisive in a way that exudes confidence. Progress is fast but assured. The drama is elevated but mindful. Characters don’t ask for permission or forgiveness; they just go after what they want, what they need, or what they feel they have to have, creating a propulsive viewing experience that zips by in a (muzzle) flash.

It’s a welcome change from prestige dramas that regularly feel like they’re stalling for time. While other reveals tout firearms around for so long it’s like they’ve never heard of Chekhov, the hunting wives pull the trigger like they’re expecting money to come out — or lovers. Before you can think, “Wait, are they gay, too?” the person in question is already bending their same-sex partner over a desk. Even Season 2’s in-media-res opening lasts only a few seconds — like it’s flipping the bird to streaming TV’s favorite plot device — giving just the briefest glimpse of cop cars racing up to a giant cabin where Margo is (supposedly) being held hostage and Sophie is (supposedly) with her, holding a gun.

Industry observers note that the opening tease only gets funnier as you find out how much unfolds between the start of the season and the flash-forward, especially considering its implication — that Sophie would threaten Margo’s life — makes sense from the start. Sophie begins Season 2 trying to repair her marriage to Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) and distance herself from Margo. The former goal sees her going to counseling sessions (where she comically compares her family to a box she wants to be trapped in), running errands, and playing the dutiful housewife.

The latter goal is harder and, arguably, more key. Margo doesn’t know her brother is dead. He’s not answering her calls or texts, but that’s hardly unprecedented behavior, so Margo ignores it — until the leader of a motorcycle gang (Dale Dickey!) demonstrates up, claiming Kyle owes her, and if he doesn’t pay, she’ll take what she wants from Margo.

According to recent reports, there’s never a good time for angry bikers to roar up your driveway demanding money, but it’s a particularly bad time for Margo. She’s in the doghouse with Jed (Dermot Mulroney) over the whole “a high schooler got me pregnant and then I had an abortion” matter, but a) that means she’s living in the pool house, not the poor house, and b) he’s really only mad because it’s a potential threat to his run for governor, which is gaining steam. Margo tries calling and texting Sophie, but she’s not answering. She wants to believe she doesn’t need Margo, love Margo, that she maybe even hates Margo. But a few cleverly laced connections make it clear she can’t.

Sources indicate that outside our core couple, Season 2 introduces plenty of plotlines that could pull them together and/or tear them apart. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) doesn’t see why welcoming a camera crew to film her friends for a reality show (“Married Justice”) could lead to problems, even when the flirty producer warns participants that they should assume they’re “always on camera.” Her husband and co-star, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box), is just as foolishly carefree, despite Deputy Wanda (Karen Rodriguez) investigating another dead girl in the woods — aka giving Callie a reason to ask questions about the last dead girl in Maple Brook, aka the aforementioned pregnant high schooler Margo killed.

It has been revealed that speaking of people Margo would prefer to forget, her former boy-toy Brad (George Ferrier), is having a hard time at Baylor. He can’t get over the recent murder of his mother, and his lonely boy coping mechanisms (playing acoustic guitar) soon attract the wrong kind of attention: a predatory music mogul named Chase (John Stamos) who promises to make Brad forget all his worries by turning him into a star (right after he loads him up with booze and drugs).

In a recent development, how Cutler shifts the puzzle pieces around to exert pressure proves just as engaging as before. There are plenty of major, loud laughs to go along with a steady supply of sly jokes and juicy melodrama. Anyone tuning in for the soap should be satisfied, just as anyone eager for some edgy satire should find it.

It has been revealed that so long as they’re as open as these characters. “The Hunting Wives” may don MAGA drag to tell its story, but it’s a savage critique of conservative values. There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

Recent findings suggest that either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover newly introduced sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

Latest Update: 'Star Trek: Deep Space Nine’s Greatest Quote Still Hasn't Been Beaten

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Star Trek: Deep Space Nine is the black sheep of the Star Trek franchise, a truth that has divided opinions ever since its debut in 1993.
  • The quote comes in the fourth episode of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine's first season: "A Man Alone." Constable Odo (René Auberjonois), Deep Space Nine's security chief, is wary of the influx of characters boarding the station via the recently discovered wormhole.
  • Recent findings suggest that that intense dislike doesn't bode well for Odo after Ibudan is found dead in one of Quark's (Armin Shimerman) holosuites.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Star Trek: Deep Space Nine is the black sheep of the Star Trek franchise, a truth that has divided opinions ever since its debut in 1993. It eschews the utopian future that was Gene Roddenberry's vision, with its enlightenment, moral fortitude, and the wonder of exploration, summed up in the "to boldly go where no man has gone before" phrase from its iconic opening narration. In its place is a gritty, darker series that takes place on a stationary outpost, where the ideal is constantly tested by moral ambiguity, subterfuge, and conflict. Nowhere is that challenge more evident than in Star Trek: Deep Space Nine's greatest quote, one made 33 years ago that began as a statement of belief in moral righteousness, only to become one of dark irony as the series progresses.

The quote comes in the fourth episode of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine's first season: "A Man Alone." Constable Odo (René Auberjonois), Deep Space Nine's security chief, is wary of the influx of characters boarding the station via the recently discovered wormhole. He takes particular offense to one, Ibudan (Stephen James Carver), who had been a smuggler of goods to Bajorans during the Cardassian Occupation. The popular opinion is that Ibudan is a hero; only Odo doesn't share that opinion. He tells Commander Sisko (Avery Brooks), after getting into a fight with Ibudan, that Ibudan had, after a young girl's parents were unable to pay for his smuggled goods, callously let her die. Strike one, in Odo's mind, and strike two came when Ibudan killed a Cardassian officer.

Recent findings suggest that that intense dislike doesn't bode well for Odo after Ibudan is found dead in one of Quark's (Armin Shimerman) holosuites. Odo is now the prime suspect, prompting Sisko to warn him that he is not to breach protocol or take the law into his own hands. Odo retorts with the series' greatest quote:.

"Laws change, depending on who's making them — Cardassians one day, Federation the next. But, justice is justice.".

In a recent development, in context, Deep Space Nine had only recently come under joint Federation-Bajoran administration following the extended, harsh occupation by the Cardassians. Odo's role, however, has not changed under the upcoming regime: he was the enforcer of the law under the Cardassians, and now he is under the joint administration. As one would expect, the written laws under Cardassian rule were far more Draconian than those of Starfleet, so the idea of what is right is fluid, depending on who's in charge. Odo, by his very nature, sees justice as an absolute principle, a standard of morality that is true and right regardless of what the powers-that-be dictate. Or, as he so elegantly says it, "Justice is justice.".

Sources indicate that history is littered with examples of government edicts that contradict what is morally right – look no further than Nazi Germany as a perfect example – so Odo is not wrong. But as the series progresses, Odo's strict adherence to order and fairness is challenged regularly, forcing him to see that his black-and-white thinking is more complicated in this gray environment. Order is only maintained by obeying the law, where justice often means breaking it: the pursuit of both is an exercise in futility.

And then things take a darkly ironic turn when Odo, a Changeling, discovers his origins in the Season 3 premiere two-parter, "The Search, Part I" and "The Search, Part II." That part of Odo that sees order as an absolute is, indeed, an innate part of his people, a fundamental principle they cling to. The part of Odo that seeks justice, however, is learned. Where Odo sees justice as an absolute, the Changelings see control as an absolute instead, and couldn't care less about justice. The quote now, then, takes on a tragic irony where, in his heritage, justice isn't justice: justice is control. And it's that learned justice that forces Odo to turn against the Changelings and return to Deep Space Nine.

The quote doesn't just apply to Odo's arc, but to the series as a whole. Laws don't apply in the face of the need for survival or to do what is just. The best example comes from Captain Sisko in "In the Pale Moonlight." In his pursuit of the greater good, he lies and schemes in order to bring the Romulans into the Dominion War. That pursuit inadvertently brings about the assassination of a Romulan senator, leaving Sisko to have to rectify how his actions brought it about and accept it, a casualty in the chase for justice. It's these types of complex narratives that tie directly, or indirectly, into Odo's quote that make Star Trek: Deep Space Nine a fuller, more mature entry in the Star Trek franchise.

RayNeo isn’t a small player making a major claim here. The company took the No. 1 spot in global AR smart glasses shipments across the first half of 2026, with 24.8% market share according to IDC and 23.9% according to Counterpoint Research.

Sources indicate that watching a movie on your iPhone is convenient, but craning your neck for a comfortable view is hardly cinematic. Having a premium AR display in sunglasses form, without packing a bulky mixed-reality headset or computing puck, opens up entirely fresh possibilities.

It has been revealed that the RayNeo GT Max and RayNeo GT connect to your device over a single USB-C cable. Instead of clunky goggles, the GT Series puts a massive virtual display — 59 degrees of field of view on GT Max, to be exact — into a sleek, understated sunglasses design that blends into coffee shops and airport lounges at just 68 to 78 grams. That single USB-C connection carries uncompressed video and powers the glasses directly: no secondary battery packs to carry, no charging anxiety, and zero wireless lag.

One thing to check before you buy: the glasses need a device that outputs video over USB-C (DisplayPort Alt Mode). That covers the iPhone 15, 16 and 17 series, Macs from 2015 onward with USB-C, iPad from the 10th generation on, and USB-C handhelds like the Steam Deck. The iPhone 16e, 17e and iPhone Air have USB-C ports but don’t output video over them, so they aren’t supported. Consoles and older Lightning devices need RayNeo’s HDMI adapter.

Sources indicate that both GT Max and GT use dual 1080p Micro-OLED panels, delivering a Full HD image to each eye with ultra-smooth 120Hz refresh rates in 2D mode. GT Max adds 38 pixels per degree, 98% DCI-P3 cinematic color coverage, and TÜV Rheinland triple eye-comfort certification. Each model offers three selectable virtual screen sizes, depending on how immersed you want to be:.

GT Max’s wider field of view provides a more expansive picture, while GT offers a featherweight design. For travel, the appeal is simple: an immaculate 307-inch personal theater that slips right into your daily bag alongside your Apple gear.

Recent findings suggest that the GT Series also functions as an instant, private external display for a USB-C Mac. That makes the glasses invaluable far beyond streaming media, especially when you need an expansive, shoulder-surfer-proof dual-monitor workspace on a flight, train, or co-working desk.

Both GT and GT Max include three native 3DoF hardware display modes, meaning you can position your virtual screen around your head:.

Because the tracking runs on dedicated silicon inside the glasses, none of it taxes the Mac or iPhone you’re plugged into. The glasses draw minimal power directly from the connected device and include a four-speaker spatial acoustic array co-tuned by Bang & Olufsen, with a directional Whisper Mode that cuts sound leakage on a plane or in an office.

GT Max also comes in three sizes based on inter-pupillary distance (IPD) — small for under 64mm, medium for 64–67mm, large for over 67mm — ensuring a tailored, comfortable fit.

Recent findings suggest that if an everyday display frame came out of Cupertino today, it would look like RayNeo iO. Rather than heavy visors, iO pairs with your iPhone through the RayNeo app to project glanceable, contextual intelligence into genuine everyday eyewear.

iO uses a high-efficiency binocular MicroLED optical engine to float high-contrast green text into your sightline, presenting a virtual image equivalent to a 33-inch screen viewed from two meters away. With peak eye-level brightness rated at 1,300 nits, reading notes and prompts stays crystal clear even under direct midday sun without occluding your real-world surroundings. The waveguide is 97% transparent and the optical engine is hidden inside the frame, so from the outside these read as ordinary glasses — most people never clock them as smart eyewear at all.

For presentations and pitches, the built-in teleprompter scrolls your notes in sync with your natural speaking cadence, so you keep your eyes locked on your audience instead of looking down at your phone. Alongside navigation, regular software updates continue to introduce new lifestyle tools, customizable notification filters, and contextual dashboard widgets that keep the hardware feeling fresh.

Recent findings suggest that rayNeo iO’s productivity tools extend that concept further with a focus on personal privacy. This is where they really shine in the Apple ecosystem. RayNeo’s ultra-slim titanium temple arms sit flush against your ears and leave them completely free, so your AirPods stay in with Spatial Audio, Transparency Mode, and Active Noise Cancellation untouched for music and calls, while iO handles your heads-up visual intelligence.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

Recent findings suggest that these upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 released at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also vital to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

9 Best Animated Witch Movies, Ranked

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Witches have been some of animation's most fascinating characters for decades, appearing as everything from terrifying supernatural villains to mischievous outsiders and young women discovering their magical abilities.
  • Recent findings suggest that some animated witches are defined by their extraordinary powers, while others are much more interesting because of their personalities, insecurities, and relationships with the people around them.
  • According to recent reports, european fairy tales, British children's literature, and North American television specials have all contributed memorable interpretations of the supernatural figure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Witches have been some of animation's most fascinating characters for decades, appearing as everything from terrifying supernatural villains to mischievous outsiders and young women discovering their magical abilities. The medium is particularly well suited to witchcraft, allowing filmmakers to bring impossible spells, enchanted forests, flying broomsticks, and elaborate magical realms to life without the limitations of live-action effects.

Recent findings suggest that some animated witches are defined by their extraordinary powers, while others are much more interesting because of their personalities, insecurities, and relationships with the people around them. Japanese animation has produced some of the genre's most celebrated examples, particularly through the work of Studio Ghibli, but the appeal of animated witchcraft extends well beyond anime.

According to recent reports, european fairy tales, British children's literature, and North American television specials have all contributed memorable interpretations of the supernatural figure. In order to keep this list focused, only movies where a witch is the protagonist or appears for a large part of the narrative are included.

In a recent development, little Witch Academia is a 25-minute short film with an inventive approach to magical-school storytelling. The film introduces Atsuko "Akko" Kagari, an ordinary girl who enrolls at Luna Nova Magical Academy after being inspired by a celebrated witch named Shiny Chariot.

In a recent development, akko's enthusiasm is considerably greater than her magical ability, which makes her a refreshing alternative to the usual effortlessly gifted fantasy protagonist. Her friendship with the more capable Lotte and Sucy provides plenty of comedy, while her determination to prove herself eventually leads to a spectacular confrontation involving a rampaging dragon.

According to recent reports, little Witch Academia’s animation is the real attraction, with exaggerated character expressions, energetic spell-casting, and beautifully choreographed action. Its success inspired a Kickstarter-funded sequel, The Enchanted Parade, and eventually a television series. Its short running time prevents it from reaching the emotional depth of the higher-ranked entries, but it's an exceptionally entertaining introduction to Akko's magical world.

According to recent reports, gilda Radner gives a wonderfully eccentric vocal performance as the titular witch in this Canadian animated Halloween special. Originally broadcast in 1978, Witch's Night Out follows a witch who wants to attend a Halloween party at her haunted mansion. When two children, Small and Tender, ask her to use magic to transform them into monsters, creating considerable chaos.

In a recent development, radner's comic timing gives the witch a mischievous personality that distinguishes her from the more threatening enchantresses found in traditional fairy tales. While the film's loose, sketchy animation gives the whole production a distinctive handmade quality.

At just 25 minutes, Witch's Night Out is a relatively modest production, but its offbeat humor, memorable character designs, and wonderfully dated disco soundtrack make it an enduring Halloween favorite. It also deserves recognition for giving children an animated witch who is more interested in having fun than frightening anybody.

Recent findings suggest that based on Julia Donaldson and Axel Scheffler's beloved picture book, Room on the Broom is one of the most charming animated witch stories ever produced. It depicts a friendly witch who repeatedly stops her broomstick journey to accommodate animals who have helped her recover various lost belongings.

Gillian Anderson voices the witch, with Timothy Spall, Simon Pegg, Rob Brydon, and Sally Hawkins among the supporting cast. The film's greatest strength is its simple understanding of kindness and cooperation, with the witch's generosity eventually becoming the very thing that saves her when a dragon threatens to eat her.

In a recent development, the adaptation also makes excellent use of the original book's illustrations, translating Scheffler's distinctive character designs into expressive computer animation. Its Oscar nomination for Best Animated Short Film and BAFTA Children's Award win were thoroughly deserved. Room on the Broom may be aimed primarily at younger viewers, but its warmth and visual charm make it an absolute delight.

According to recent reports, this charming Czechoslovak and West German animated fantasy deserves considerably more international recognition. Based on Otfried Preußler's children's book, The Little Witch follows a young enchantress who desperately wants to attend the witches' annual gathering on Walpurgis Night. Unfortunately, she's considered too young by the other witches, who give her a year to prove herself worthy of joining them.

Accompanied by her raven Abraxas, the Little Witch sets about learning how to become a good witch. However, her unconventional understanding of witchcraft eventually brings her into conflict with the established magical authorities.

It has been revealed that the distinctive animation gives The Little Witch a wonderfully folkloric atmosphere, while its central character offers an appealing alternative to the traditional wicked witch. Rather than celebrating magical power for its own sake, the story considers what makes somebody good and whether authority deserves unquestioning obedience. Though hampered by its limited budget, the combination of European folklore, gentle humor, and rebellious spirit makes it one of the most interesting entries here.

Recent findings suggest that walt Disney Animation Studios returns to witchcraft with Hexed, an original magical coming-of-age adventure featuring Hailee Steinfeld as Billie Doe. An unconventional teenager who has never quite fitted in, Billie discovers that she possesses extraordinary magical abilities, transporting herself from suburban life into the fantastical witch realm of Hexe.

The supporting voice cast is particularly impressive, including Jodie Foster as the sinister Queen Celeste, Walton Goggins as a magical three-eyed cat, and Stephen Fry as an enchanted journal.

Hexed has an appealing mother-daughter relationship at its center, giving its magical adventure an emotional dimension beyond the usual discovery-of-powers storyline. Its elaborate fantasy setting and colorful supernatural characters also make it a particularly exciting addition to Disney's animated catalog. It hasn't yet had the time to establish the legacy of the classics above it, but its premise and creative ambition earn it a place among the genre's most promising modern entries.

Studio Ponoc's first feature film has plenty of the magical wonder associated with its creators' previous work at Studio Ghibli. Based on Mary Stewart's 1971 novel The Little Broomstick, Mary And The Witch's Flower follows Mary Smith, a young girl who discovers a mysterious flower that blooms once every seven years. Its magical properties temporarily grant her extraordinary abilities, allowing her to fly on a broomstick and gain admission to the mysterious Endor College.

Industry observers note that director Hiromasa Yonebayashi previously worked on Spirited Away and directed The Secret World of Arrietty and When Marnie Was There. His experience is evident in the film's gorgeous environments, expressive character animation, and imaginative magical sequences.

Its story occasionally relies on familiar fantasy conventions, and at times can feel quite narratively thin. However, Mary and the Witch's Flower captures the excitement of discovering a world where almost anything is possible through utterly entrancing visuals.

Belladonna of Sadness is easily the most adult and disturbing film on this list. The experimental Japanese animation follows Jeanne, a peasant woman who turns to the Devil after suffering horrific abuse at the hands of her feudal lord. Her supernatural bargain gradually transforms her into a powerful witch, but her growing influence threatens the patriarchal authorities who control the community.

As Jeanne gains confidence and power, the film develops into a provocative exploration of female sexuality, oppression, and rebellion. Visually, Belladonna of Sadness is unlike almost anything else in animation. Its watercolor imagery, elaborate compositions, and psychedelic sequences frequently resemble moving illustrations rather than conventional cartoons.

Sources indicate that much of Belladonna Of Sadness uses limited animation, allowing its artwork to carry the emotional weight of the story. The sexual violence and explicit imagery make it emphatically unsuitable for younger audiences, but its audacious artistic direction and unconventional feminist themes make it one of the most enchanting animated witch films ever produced.

Spirited Away is rightly considered one of the greatest animated films ever made, and its central antagonist is one of animation's most memorable witches. When ten-year-old Chihiro becomes trapped in the spirit world, she must find work at a gigantic bathhouse operated by Yubaba, a formidable sorceress who steals her employees' names and exercises extraordinary control over their lives.

According to recent reports, yubaba is a brilliant creation. Her enormous head, extravagant appearance, and terrifying magical abilities make her immediately imposing. The film's witchcraft is also woven into its wider exploration of Japanese folklore, with Yubaba's bathhouse populated by spirits, strange creatures, and supernatural visitors. Chihiro's survival does not depend on learning magical abilities, but rather developing courage, compassion, and resourcefulness.

It has been revealed that winner of the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, Spirited Away is a truly extraordinary achievement in storytelling and animation. Yubaba alone makes it essential viewing for anyone interested in animated witches, even if the film's brilliance extends far beyond its supernatural antagonist.

Hayao Miyazaki's Kiki's Delivery Service is the definitive animated witch movie because it understands that magic is often most interesting when examining everyday life. Based on Eiko Kadono's novel, it depicts 13-year-old Kiki, who leaves home with her talking black cat Jiji to complete a traditional year of independent living.

It has been revealed that with flying as her only magical skill, she establishes an aerial delivery service from a local bakery, gradually building friendships and discovering the responsibilities of adulthood. However, her magical abilities aren't unlimited, and the pressures of independence eventually cause her to lose her ability to fly.

Industry observers note that rather than relying on a conventional villain or world-threatening magical crisis, Kiki's Delivery Service is built around a relatable experience of adolescence: losing confidence in something that once came naturally. The animation is beautiful, particularly the detailed European-inspired city and the expressive sequences of Kiki flying above its rooftops. Other animated films might feature more powerful witches or more elaborate displays of magic, but few capture the wonder of being a young witch quite as convincingly as Kiki's Delivery Service.

How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, every visual element in animation helps tell the story.
  • According to recent reports, and by “more,” we mean witches.
  • In a recent development, “Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something new inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

According to recent reports, and by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

In a recent development, “Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

Sources indicate that according to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”.

Recent findings suggest that but the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

In a recent development, “The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”.

Recent findings suggest that billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

Recent findings suggest that both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn stated. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”.

“What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”.

Recent findings suggest that one key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”.

Recent findings suggest that but Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie stated yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”.

Bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”.

According to recent reports, leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush said. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”.

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush said.

“Hexed” is now playing in theaters.

Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials.
  • All of this could potentially be put at risk by the organization’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….
  • Recent findings suggest that apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging.

All of this could potentially be put at risk by the organization’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….

Recent findings suggest that apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect. For example, when it claimed that the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 were carbon neutral back in 2023, that claim was described as “bogus,” with the EU banning Apple from repeating it. The tech giant has also been criticized for pushing a relentless annual iPhone cycle, encouraging frequent upgrades.

Industry observers note that overall, however, Apple has first-rate credentials when it comes to the environment. It was way back in 2018 when the company hit its goal of running its own operations off 100% renewable energy. This includes all Apple facilities, from Apple Park through data centers to its worldwide retail store network.

I said at the time that using more environmentally friendly packaging should be the manufacturer’s next priority, and it has indeed made great progress with this over the years, succeeding in removing all plastic packaging earlier this year.

It has been revealed that after its own operations, Apple set about trying to tackle the power usage of its manufacturing partners. Back in 2020, the company set a goal of having its entire supply chain be carbon neutral by 2030. Just four years later, Apple said it was 95% of the way there.

The firm also helps fund and support a wide range of environmental initiatives around the world. Just a few examples include conservation in China’s national parks, environmental protection and carbon removal in Australia and Newly introduced Zealand, and helping to fund the build-out of renewable energy capacity in India.

Potentially, however, the vast energy demands of the data centers powering AI services could put its 2030 goal at risk. Other tech giants have already admitted that it may lead them to fail to hit their own renewable energy promises.

Back in 2024, for example, Google CEO Sundar Pichai mentioned that the AI boom was “challenging” to the organization’s 2030 carbon-free goal. CNET reports that Meta is now also admitting that it may fail to hit the same target.

Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the tech giant is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline.”.

Notably, a lot of Siri’s most advanced AI capabilities are currently powered by Google’s Gemini models.

Sources indicate that at the same 2024 event where Google expressed doubts, Apple reiterated its commitment to its 2030 target. Then-CEO Tim Cook repeated this assurance later the same year, although admitted it would be challenging.

More challenges, yes. But are we coming off the goal? No, definitely not. With more data centers, you use more renewable energy, and we’ve built that muscle now […] I feel very good about 2030.

In the company’s most recent environmental progress report, it said that it was was still using 100% renewable energy despite using over 2.5 billion kWh of electricity to power its data centers.

Industry observers note that we’re proud that 100 percent of that electricity came from renewable sources including solar, wind, and low-impact hydropower. To cover our needs, we build our own renewable power projects and work with utilities to purchase clean energy from locally obtained resources. We’re staying at 100 percent even as Apple’s data center capacity continues to grow.

The same report noted the company had achieved zero water use for cooling at its latest data centers.

At our three newest data centers, we use high-efficiency air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled systems, resulting in zero water use for cooling.

It has been revealed that however, the greatest challenge for Apple lies ahead. The reason that Google and Meta are now backtracking on their promises is that both companies now have massive AI capabilities. As yet, Apple does not.

What happens as Apple expands Siri AI capabilities as usage increases, and as the company moves into agentic AI features? Is it realistic for the company to maintain its 100% track record with vastly greater data center energy usage?

Greenpeace expressed its own doubts earlier this year.

Industry observers note that “AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” spokesperson Avex Li indicates. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the tech giant will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”.

Apple did not respond directly but merely pointed to its past statements and most recent environmental progress report.

I don’t doubt the company’s desire to maintain its track record, but if Apple does join the likes of Google and Meta in becoming a major AI player, sticking to its 2030 timing is going to become increasingly difficult.

After two months of expecting the worst and hoping for the best, Outlander: Blood of My Blood Season 2 ends in less than 24 hours. A prequel to the hit series Outlander, the historical fantasy drama explores the love stories of two couples who lived long before Jamie and Claire Fraser's romance began. Rather than adapting Diana Gabaldon's novels directly, the series expands the Outlander universe by focusing on the parents of its central characters: Jamie's parents, Brian Fraser (Jamie Roy) and Ellen MacKenzie (Harriet Slater), and Claire's parents, Henry Beauchamp (Jeremy Irvine) and Julia Moriston (Hermione Corfield).

Before Outlander wrapped up its eight-season run in May 2026, Blood of My Blood premiered on August 8, 2025. The first season concluded after ten episodes on October 10, 2025, but the network had already renewed the gripping drama for a second season in June, ahead of the finale. Season 2 premiered on September 18, 2026, and though it is already approaching its tenth and final episode, a third season has yet to be greenlit. This begs the question: Is this the end for Outlander: Blood of My Blood? Well, it's still too early to say, since TV highlights often get renewed later than anticipated.

With that, the Season 2 finale of Outlander: Blood of My Blood, titled "Twelfth Night," is scheduled to premiere tomorrow, November 27, amid the Thanksgiving break. The episode airs on Starz at 8 p.m. ET, where new episodes have premiered weekly since the romance series debuted. This comes two weeks after a scheduled pause in the Season 2 schedule, as no new episode aired on November 13, after eight straight weeks of releases.

Sources indicate that four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

In a recent development, you belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

According to recent reports, the penultimate episode, "Another Man's Shadow," leads directly into the Blood of My Blood finale, offering some much-needed answers while raising even more questions. A "Twelfth Night" preview has also been released, hinting at high-stakes danger and a festive titular gathering (referencing Shakespeare's Twelfth Night) that turns violent, setting the stage for a potentially shocking cliffhanger.

It has been revealed that speaking with Collider about the challenges their characters face this season on Outlander: Blood of My Blood, Corfield and Irvine teased that the finale will leave fans eager for a potential third season, thanks to that cliffhanger. However, Corfield admitted that she is uncertain about Julia's fate and what might happen next. "I don't know what's coming next, to be completely honest, from where the season ends," she mentioned. "We have no idea. It could go anywhere … We're either hanging in the balance or being tortured.".

The final episode of Outlander: Blood of My Blood Season 2 airs on Starz tomorrow. Watch the teaser above.
